Υποθέτοντας προσδόκιμο ζωής o…
items.descriptionOriginal: In a 2023 TEDx Talk at Laguna Blanca School, Dino Ambrosi made a startling revelation that perfectly underlines the big question of the smartphone era: What is my time worth? Ambrosi is the founder of Project Reboot and an expert at guiding teens and young adults to develop more empowering relationships with technology. Assuming a life expectancy of 90 (an optimistic estimate, since U.S. life expectancy is currently 79 ), and after calculating the average time they spend sleeping, going to school, working, driving, cooking, eating, doing chores, and taking care of personal hygiene , today’s 18-year-olds have only 334 months of their adult lives to themselves. “How you spend this time will determine the quality of your life,” Ambrosi says. However, given the tech habits of today’s young people, most of those months will be spent staring at screens, leaving them with just 22 months to make their mark on the world. “Today, the average 18-year-old in the United States is on pace to spend 93% of their remaining free time looking at a screen,” Ambrosi says. An 18-year-old’s remaining time, in months. Photo credit: TEDx The idea that an entire generation will spend most of their free time in front of screens is chilling. However, the message has a silver lining. Sharing this information with young people can immediately impact how they spend their time. How to get teens to reduce their screen time Ambrosi says his work with Project Reboot through on-campus initiatives, school assemblies, and parent workshops has taught him that teens are more concerned about time wasted on their phones than the damage it may do to their mental health. Knowing which topic resonates can open the door to an effective dialogue about a topic that’s hard for many young people to discuss. When teens realize they are giving away their entire lives for free, they are more likely to reconsider their relationship with smartphones. “I actually don’t get through to a lot of teens, as well as when I help them realize the value of their time and then highlight the fact that that time is being stolen from them,” Ambrosi told Upworthy . A Common Sense Media study shows that, as of 2021, the average 13- to 18-year-old spent 8 hours and 39 minutes a day on entertainment screen time, not counting school or homework. “It’s important to get them to view time as their most valuable resource that they can use to invest in themselves or enjoy life and tick the boxes on their bucket list. I really want them to see that it’s something they should take control of and prioritize, because we’re all under the impression that social media is free, but it’s actually not. We just pay for it with our time.” Dino Ambrosi speaks at a school assembly. Photo credit: Dino Ambrosi (used with permission) Ambrosi believes that young people are less likely to give their time to tech companies for free when they understand the value of their time. “I find that kids really respond to that message because nobody wants to feel manipulated, right? And giving them that sense of being wronged, which I think they have been, by tech companies that are off operating on business models that are not aligned with their well-being, is important.” His approach to getting teens to rethink their smartphone use is similar to that of the Truth Initiative in that it educates young people about the nefarious tactics big tobacco companies used to lure and addict young people. In a way, big tech companies are doing the same thing by luring young people into their products, connecting them with friends and influencers, while providing a product that the U.S. Surgeon General warned in 2023 can pose a profound risk of harm to young people’s mental health. He also believes parents should be sympathetic and nonjudgmental when talking to young people about screen time because it’s a struggle that just about everyone faces and feels ashamed about. A little understanding will prevent them from shutting down the conversation altogether. How to reduce my screen time Ambrosi has some suggestions to help people reduce their screen time: The ClearSpace app ClearSpace forces you to take a breathing delay before using a distracting app. It also asks you to set a time limit and allows you to set a number of visits to the site per day. If you eclipse the number of visits, it sends a text to a friend saying you exceeded your budget. This can help people hold one another accountable for their screen time goals. Don’t sleep with your phone Ambrosi says to charge your phone far away from your bedside stand when you sleep and use an alarm clock to wake up. If you do have an alarm clock on your phone, set up an automation so that as soon as you turn off the alarm, it opens up an app like Flora or Forest and starts an hour-long timer that incentivizes you to be off your phone for the first hour of the day. “In my experience, if you can stay off screens for the last hour and the first hour of the day, the other 22 hours get a lot easier because you get the quality rest and sleep that you need to wake up fully charged, and now you’re more capable of being intentional because you are at your best,” Ambrosi told Upworthy . A teen boy looks at his phone in bed. Photo credit: Canva Keep apps in one place Ambrosi says to keep all of your social apps and logins on one device. “I try to designate a specific use for each device as much as possible,” he told Upworthy . “I try to keep all my social media time and all my entertainment on my phone as opposed to my computer because I want my computer to be a tool for work.” Kids are waking up to the problem Even though there are significant challenges ahead for young people as they try to navigate a screen-based world while keeping screens at a healthy distance, Ambrosi was optimistic about the future when he first spoke with Upworthy for this story. “I’m really optimistic because I have seen in the last year, in particular, that the receptiveness of student audiences has increased by almost an order of magnitude. Kids are waking up to the fact that this is the problem. They want to have this conversation,” he told Upworthy . “Some clubs are starting to address this problem at several schools right now; from the talks I’ve given this semester alone, kids want to be involved in this conversation. They’re creating phone-free spaces on college and high school campuses by their own accord. I just think we have a huge potential to leverage this moment to move things in the right direction.” Since this story first ran, the phone-free movement has gone mainstream: Education Week counts about 30 states with bell-to-bell school phone bans , and several more restrict phones during class. For more information on Ambrosi’s programs , visit ProjectReboot.School. visit ProjectReboot.School. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Tech expert shares the one message that actually convinces teens to reconsider their screen time appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ζευγάρι φυτεύει το πραγματικό «δέντρο του χρήματος» και οι πρώτοι σπόροι του αξίζουν πάνω από 6.700 δολάρια
items.titleOriginal: Couple plants real-life ‘money tree’ and its first seeds are worth over $6,700
items.description: Όπως λέει η παλιά παροιμία, τα χρήματα δεν φυτρώνουν στα δέντρα. Ωστόσο, τι θα γινόταν αν είχατε ένα δέντρο που ήταν τόσο σπάνιο που οι άνθρωποι θα ξόδευαν καλά χρήματα για τους σπόρους του; Τότε θα μπορούσατε να πείτε ειλικρινά ότι έχετε ένα δέντρο χρημάτων που φυτρώνει στην αυλή σας. Αυτό συμβαίνει με ένα ζευγάρι συνταξιούχων στην Αγγλία, την Pamela και τον Alistair Thompson, τότε και οι δύο 75 ετών, που το 2010 πλήρωσαν 70 £ (98 $).…
items.descriptionOriginal: As the old adage goes, money doesn’t grow on trees. However, what if you had a tree that was so rare that people would spend good money for its seeds? Then you could honestly say that you have a money tree growing in your yard . Such is the case for a retired couple in England, Pamela and Alistair Thompson, then both 75, who in 2010 paid £70 ($98) for a 46cm-tall Wollemi pine sapling that a friend bought on the Shopping Channel. It’s believed that it was the first ever endangered tree species to be protected by making it available to the general public . What is the Wollemi pine? The Wollemi pine is valuable because its lineage stretches back some 200 million years, and it was thought to have gone extinct about 2 million years ago. However, in 1994, park ranger David Noble came across a Wollemi pine in a secluded gorge in Australia. Biologically, it was a discovery as significant as coming across a living dinosaur in a hidden part of Australia in the ‘90s. Wollemi is an Australian Aboriginal word that means “watch out, look around you.” A Wollemi pine in Seattle, Washington. Photo credit: Brewbooks/Wikimedia Commons The tree may have made its way to Eurpoe, but the wild trees are under threat from wildfires and climate change. It’s believed that only about 90 exist in the wild today. In 2005, it made its European debut when Sir David Attenborough planted one at the Royal Botanic Gardens in Kew. “How exciting we should discover this rare survivor from such an ancient past,” Attenborough said. After 15 years of special care, the Thompson’s tree began to produce cones for the first time in August 2025. “This year has been so ­unusually dry, it happened earlier,” she said, according to The Times . The couple planned to package the valuable seeds from the tree and give the money to the National Garden Scheme . The National Garden Scheme is a charity where people open their gardens up to the general public, and the money raised is donated to nursing and health charities, including the Queen’s Institute of Community Nursing. How much does a Wollemi pine cost? “I saw a small tree for sale for more than £1,000 ($1,352), which shows how rare they are. We’re planning to package the seeds five or six at a time and sell the bundles online for £5 ($6.76). We’ve seen some retailers sell them for much more, but we want to make them accessible for people, as well as raise money for charity. We don’t yet know how many will be healthy and produce trees. Only time will tell.” “We have around five large cones, which have produced about a hundred or so large seeds each. It would be lovely to see just how many seeds we can produce, but I have been very surprised by the numbers so far this year,” she said, according to Unilad . So, if you do the math, 100 seed packs at $6.76 each would go for $676. Not bad for just collecting seeds. But they could make a lot more money off the seeds if they chose to do so. It’s believed that one seed can go for as much as £10 ($13.52). If they sold all 500 seeds produced by the five cones, they’d make $6,760. If the tree keeps producing cones, it could bring in thousands of dollars more in the coming years. “It really does prove that money can grow on trees,” Mr. Thompson said, according to The Times . A female Wollemi pine cone. Photo credit: Adrian198cm/Wikimedia Commons Preserving the Wollemi pine for the future In 2023, over 170 young Wollemi pines grown by the Botanic Gardens of Sydney, in Australia, were shipped to be planted in 28 botanic gardens with climates that could support the pines, across the UK and Europe. A separate collection was also sent to a botanic garden in Atlanta, Georgia, in the U.S. “Discovering the lost Wollemi pines in the wild was a truly astounding moment for international tree conservation, and to be a leading partner nearly thirty years later in launching this important new metacollection on UK soil is an exciting moment for Forestry England,” Mike Seddon, Forestry England Chief Executive, said in a press release . “As we care for the Wollemi pines we plant today, we’ll be able to study the way they grow, learning with the other botanic gardens how they flourish outside Australia. The climate crisis means that across all continents, many trees like Wollemi pines are facing urgent threats to their survival. We know that 34 per cent of conifers are now endangered, and our ongoing work to research, propagate, and save tree species is more vital than ever.” This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Couple plants real-life ‘money tree’ and its first seeds are worth over $6,700 appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: 9 common English words and phrases that take on entirely different meanings in England
items.description: Ο Evan Edinger, ένας Αμερικανο-Βρετανός YouTuber που ζει στο Λονδίνο και μοιράζεται συχνά παιχνιδιάρικες συγκρίσεις μεταξύ της ζωής στις δύο χώρες, τόνισε πώς ακόμη και οι προσεγγίσεις στη μητρική γλώσσα μπορεί να διαφέρουν πολύ. Και δεν μιλάμε για «ασανσέρ» έναντι «ασανσέρ» ή «τηγανητές πατάτες» έναντι «τσιπς» εδώ. Ακόμη και όροι που φαίνονται καθολικοί μεταξύ των αγγλόφωνων μπορούν να tu…
items.descriptionOriginal: Evan Edinger, an American-British YouTuber living in London who often shares playful comparisons between life in the two countries, highlighted how even approaches to the mother tongue can vary widely . And we’re not talking about “lifts” versus “elevators” or “fries” versus “chips” here. Even terms that seem universal among English speakers can turn out to mean entirely different things . “English is full of words that quietly flip meaning when you cross the Atlantic. Words that you think sound polite…[but] can really land you in hot water if you use them across the pond,” Edinger said in a now-viral video, before listing some of the most surprising ones he’s come across while living abroad. Read below and see if there’s an innocent phrase you use often that could be met with furrowed brows should you ever go on a jaunt in jolly old England. Here are 9 words that quietly flip meaning 1. Quite good Using a graph from YouGov, Edinger showed how in the UK, “quite good” actually ranks lower than “good,” meaning something “quite good” is worse than something “good.” It’d be the same as saying something is “fairly good,” or just so-so. Conversely, in America, it’s often used as an intensifier to denote something “better than good.” As Edinger put it: “American ‘quite’ and British ‘quite’ are quite the opposite.” View this post on Instagram 2. With all due respect If you ever hear a Brit say this, Edinger warns that “they do not mean it.” It’s really just a polite, passive-aggressive way of saying “you’re an idiot, and I think you’re full of sh*t.” To be fair, plenty of Americans use “with all due respect” to preface remarks that are anything but respectful. But you get the gist. 3. Thanks, I’ll bear that in mind Many Brits use “I’ll bear that in mind” as an indirect refusal, while Americans are more likely to mean it sincerely. The ones that cause the most confusion 4. To “table” something Edinger noted that this phrase is a particular source of confusion between Americans and Brits. In the UK, to “table” a discussion means to put it on the agenda for discussion. Americans, by contrast, use it synonymously with “shelving” something, saving a less important topic for a later date, or better yet, never mentioning it again. 5. Moot point Originally, a “moot point” was something brought up in a public assembly or court . Brits have held onto this meaning, so when something is “moot,” it’s an open question worth debating. However, in America, Edinger says, a moot point is “usually something completely irrelevant,” because the opportunity to act on it has passed. 6. Solicitor Americans might associate the word with a “door-to-door salesman…or a prostitute,” Edinger quipped. In the UK, however, a “solicitor” is one of the two main types of practicing lawyer in England and Wales (the other is a barrister), a legal professional who provides specialized legal advice. As an American, you might be wondering, why not just call them lawyer s ? In the UK, however, “lawyer” is a broad term for anyone who works in law, without the same formal qualifications implied by “solicitor.” 7. Public school Public schools in America are free and government-funded, and are the source of many debates among parents and educators for that very reason. In the UK, however, “public school” refers to a small group of long-established, fee-charging schools, many of them boarding schools, the most famous of which is Eton College. “State school” would be used to describe what Americans know as a “public school.” Bonkers. 8. Momentarily To an American, this means “ in a moment.” To a Brit, it means “ for a moment.” The real-world implication of this discrepancy really shines in Edinger’s pilot analogy. If a Brit heard that their plane would be “landing momentarily,” it might suggest touching down on the tarmac only briefly before going back up. Hope you don’t have a connecting flight! 9. Not bad Edinger explained that while “not bad” could mean “good” to a Brit, he thinks it’s another tool for understating true feeling. In that sense, “not bad” can mean anything a little better than good, much like how Americans tend to interpret “quite good.” What this list actually tells us Language is one of those things that feels completely universal right up until the moment it isn’t. If you and a British colleague are in a meeting and you suggest “tabling” something, you could walk out of that room with completely opposite understandings of what just happened. And if they told you your idea was “quite good,” you might feel great about it while they quietly file it in the bin. The deeper point is that politeness, directness, and even respect don’t translate the way we assume they do, and that’s worth knowing before you board the plane. You can follow Evan Edinger on YouTube and Instagram . This article originally appeared in January. It has been updated. The post 9 common English words and phrases that take on entirely different meanings in England appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Most people can learn most things if they really put their minds to it, but there’s no question some humans are born with innate abilities that defy expectations and explanation. We call those people prodigies , and while toddlerhood might be too early to definitively use that label, a tiny tot with a stick, a shovel, and a song in his heart has people tossing around the term. When you see the video of little Remi performing Natasha Bedingfield’s “Pocketful of Sunshine,” you’ll see why. Toddlers often “sing” along to songs, but rarely do they sing with anything close to perfect pitch and even more rarely do they keep perfect time. Not only does Remi do both, but he keeps separate rhythms with each hand (a plastic sandbox shovel in one, a stick in the other) while singing gibberish lyrics to the identifiable tune. Watch: Viewers couldn’t believe their ears Not a discernible word uttered, yet so very impressive. People had thoughts: “He’s singing in Simlish lmao so cute also more talent than me” “The gibberish in perfect melody is killing meeee I love smart babies “ “Mee me may mayyyyy!” “Forget about the singing, he’s playing two different rhythms with each hand. Mind blown seriously.” “Holding down a beat and singing at that age is insane!!!!!” “I am literally astonished. memorizing melody, singing it back with the correct notes on key?! While drumming??? Literal prodigy in the making.” “When they say some people are just born with it- this is what that looks like. Absolutely amazing.” “Can’t poop in the potty but can perfectly replicate a song “ “It’s actually so hard to sing and drum.” “I think he’s a prodigy. Very impressive!” Even the pros are impressed Even trained musicians weighed in on this little pocketful of sunshine’s talents. “I am a highly trained musician. He is…a natural percussionist. He also sings incredibly well for his age. This kid has music pouring out of him. He can pattern phrases and complicated rhythms.” “I’ve been drumming for 26 years. Dude is a natural and has exquisite dynamic control. And he can sing on top? Brilliant! ” “Vocal coach here. He can even hear vocal dynamics (the volume increases and decreases in his singing) and is able to actively apply them WHILE keeping a complicated rhythm for his age…you guys might have a prodigy. Your son is remembering the beat, Melody and dynamics…you guys might want to get him a coach!!” “I’m a music teacher, and his natural ability to figure out the beat and keep it, is something I struggle teaching kids who have been playing for years. little prodigy in the making friends, get him into lessons!!” Many people suggested getting him a drum set and a coach. The drum set is already taken care of. Santa brought him one for Christmas, and he plays it a lot. Remi’s mom Jessica writes in a comment that Remi started showing signs that he loved drumming and was able to carry a beat at around age 2 1/2. (In the drumset video above, he’s 3 years and 4 months.) Jessica also shares that Remi has a special affinity for Elvis Presley. He even told her, “Mama, Remi the real Elvis!” He may very well be. Where does talent like this come from? Musical prodigies usually arise from some combination of nature and nurture, possessing an inherent musical capacity and being raised in an environment that feeds that ability. Some have tried to argue that anyone can become a “prodigy” with enough early exposure and systematic practice, but that doesn’t really explain kids like Remi. You can’t teach the average two or three-year-old to drum with both hands playing different beats while keeping steady time, and while singing in tune with inflections, at least not without a ton of work. When an ability appears without much effort, that sure seems to be an indicator of innate talent. Any talent has to be nurtured and practice is necessary, of course, but there are lots of kids who start music lessons and practice at a young age who don’t become Mozarts by age seven. One 2020 study found that what differentiated musical prodigies from other young musicians was a propensity to report “flow” during practice, the intensity of their practice before adolescence, and the source of their motivation when they began to play. Perhaps it’s just a matter of all the elements coming together: innate capacity, a tendency to get lost in the music, intense early practice, and some intangible thing that makes the musical magic happen. Wherever musical prodigy comes from, it’s sure fun to see it emerging in such a tiny little human. Remi’s big moment at the Opry Remi’s future has already included a big moment. In December 2025, then-3-year-old Remi Steinert won a social media contest to join the band for KING + COUNTRY onstage at the Grand Ole Opry, where he played “Little Drummer Boy” on Dec. 16. He is believed to be the youngest musician ever to perform at the Opry , according to local station KMTV, and his family later shared the moment with the 16th Air Force. Now 4, Remi still shares his drumming on TikTok. Can’t wait to see what else Remi’s future holds. You can follow Remi’s musical adventures on TikTok . This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Precocious toddler drums and sings ‘Pocketful of Sunshine’ with stunning precision appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve ever moved a bit of food off your own plate just so your dog could eat, too, then you know the feeling this program is trying to address. It’s a pretty common one in New York City right now. And most people who surrender a pet to a shelter aren’t doing it lightly. They do it as the very last resort, when they’ve truly run out of ways to make it work. NYC has put $500,000 toward the problem. The city is funding 22 food pantries across all five boroughs to stock and distribute free pet food, with supplies expected to start arriving within about two weeks. Teddy and everyone like him Cassandra, a Brooklyn resident, has a three-year-old Shih Tzu named Teddy, who she’s had since he was two months old. “Sometimes I have to sacrifice a little of my food that way he doesn’t go hungry, until I can get more food for him,” she said. At The Campaign Against Hunger in Brooklyn, pantry director Tamara Dawson has watched the same dynamic for years. “They bring their pets with them and are feeding them online because they have been without,” she said. The organization already offers free pet food to clients, but the supply has always depended on chasing grants and donors. The city funding makes that a little less precarious. What happened after SNAP cuts St. John’s Bread and Life in Brooklyn received a $17,000 voucher through the initiative. Staff said demand has grown since many clients saw their SNAP benefits reduced, something that moved through the whole household budget , pets included. “The affordability crisis affects every member of a family, including the pets we love,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “No New Yorker should have to choose between feeding themselves and feeding their pets.” Animal welfare groups have tracked the connection between financial hardship and shelter surrender for years. Getting pet food to families early is a pretty practical way to keep that from happening. Where to find free pet food in NYC Here are all 22 participating locations: Bronx – Part of the Solution: 2759 Webster Ave., 10458 – New York Common Pantry: 1290 Hoe Ave., 10459 – Davidson Community Center: 2038 Davidson Ave., 10453 – The Kingsbridge Heights Community Center: 3067 Kingsbridge Terrace, 10463 Queens – First United Methodist Church of Jamaica: 162-10 Highland Ave., 11432 – River Fund: 89-11 Lefferts Boulevard, 11418 – Yeshua Worldwide Ministries Food Pantry: 7911 Caldwell Ave., 11379 – Hour Children Community Outreach: 36-49 11th Street, 11106 Brooklyn – Community Help in Park Slope: 200 Fourth Ave., 11217 – Metropolitan Council on Jewish Poverty: 5361 Preston Court, 11234 – On the Go Relief: 2832 Fulton Street, 11207 – St. John’s Bread and Life Food Pantry: 795 Lexington Ave., 11221 – The Campaign Against Hunger: 2004 Fulton Street, 11233 – YMCA Community Market: 2980 West 29th Street, 11224 Manhattan – Holy Apostles Soup Kitchen Pantry: 296 Ninth Ave., 10001 – New York Common Pantry: 8 East 109th Street, 10029 – St. Clemens Food Pantry: 423 West 46th Street, 10036 – The Father’s Heart Ministries: 543-545 East 11th Street, 10009 – The Lower Eastside Girls Club: 402 East 8th Street, 10009 – Trinity’s Services and Food for the Homeless: 602 East 9th Street, 10009 Staten Island – Project Hospitality: 205 Canal Street, 10304 – Feeding with TLC: 309 St. Paul’s Ave., 10304 Call ahead if you’re not sure what to bring or whether your nearest location is stocked yet. And if someone you know could use this, it’s the kind of thing that’s good to pass along. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΑΙΣΙΟΔΟΞΟΥ Το Halloween μπορεί να είναι η μία νύχτα το χρόνο που όλη η οικογένεια καταλήγει έξω μαζί, μετακινούμενος στη γειτονιά στο σκοτάδι. Το αν αυτό τελειώνει με μαγεία ή κατάρρευση εξαρτάται σχεδόν αποκλειστικά από το αν η εμπειρία ταιριάζει με το παιδί που φέρατε μαζί σας. Η Dr. Kristen Cook, πιστοποιημένη παιδίατρος…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Halloween might be the one night a year when the whole family ends up outside together, moving through the neighborhood in the dark. Whether that ends in magic or meltdown depends almost entirely on whether the experience matches the kid you brought with you. Dr. Kristen Cook , a board-certified pediatrician with more than 15 years of practice in the Midwest, writes that across every age, Halloween offers genuine opportunities to practice life skills like facing fears, managing expectations, developing independence, and showing kindness. How much kids are able to glean out spooky season depends on how you set it up. Toddlers and preschoolers: small excursion, low stimulation The tricky thing about Halloween for little kids is that everything exciting about it is also a lot. Unfamiliar noises, scary decorations , a neighborhood full of costumed kids running in every direction; it can tip from exciting to overwhelming fast. Dr. Cook’s rule for this age: comfortable over elaborate. Costumes shouldn’t restrict movement or vision, and there’s no reason to push through the full neighborhood circuit after dark. An early start, before it gets busy, tends to go better. Bring a wagon or stroller even if your toddler insists they don’t need one because, let’s face it, they probably will. Inspect every piece of candy before it’s touched, check for choking hazards and allergens, and agree on a daily candy limit in advance so it’s not a negotiation every time. And if the evening tips into over-stimulation, head home. A short, good Halloween beats a long, tearful one. School-age kids: independence with eyes on Elementary-age kids are ready for more. They can choose their own costumes, help decorate the house, pick out pumpkins , and have real opinions about the trick-or-treating route. Dr. Cook recommends mapping that route together in advance and letting kids take the lead once you’re out. That said, supervision doesn’t disappear. Pumpkin carving is still an adult activity at this age, and a parent or trusted adult should remain part of the outing, even if they’re hanging back a house or two. Night-friendly costume details matter more here. Think glow bracelets, LED accessories, and reflective elements. The shift at this stage is toward earned independence. Let them decide who they trick-or-treat with. Let them handle their own candy negotiations. Keep the safety guardrails in place, but make room for them to feel the difference. Teenagers: expectations and exit plans By the teenage years, Halloween looks different. Some teens feel too old for trick-or-treating; others still want to be part of it. Dr. Cook’s take is not to push them out of it. Teenagers who help hand out candy, look after younger siblings, or supervise part of the evening have a real role that doesn’t require a costume. If they’re going out independently, the conversations to have are about curfew, approved locations, and what to do if they end up somewhere uncomfortable. Dr. Cook specifically recommends creating an exit plan before they leave, so they have a way out of an uncomfortable situation without needing to explain themselves in the moment. A standing offer of a no-questions pickup goes a long way. The bigger ask for teenagers is respect. Taking more than a reasonable amount from an unattended candy bowl, or pulling pranks that leave families upset, isn’t harmless fun. Dr. Cook frames this as a chance to practice the kind of independence that looks like actual maturity. What all ages have in common The memories that stick, Dr. Cook writes, usually aren’t about the costumes or the candy. They’re about the feelings that are attached to them. They remember feeling included, connected, part of something. Halloween doesn’t require expensive gear or elaborate setups. It requires showing up for the kid in front of you, at whatever stage they’re at. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . Αυτές οι δύο γενιές έζησαν τη Μεγάλη Ύφεση και τον Δεύτερο Παγκόσμιο Πόλεμο, δύο γεγονότα που ανάγκασαν τους Αμερικανούς να γίνουν περισσότεροι…
items.descriptionOriginal: For those with great grandparents, grandparents, and parents from the Greatest Generation (those born 1901 to 1927) and the Silent Generation (those born 1928 to 1945), much can be learned from how to live a frugal lifestyle . These two generations lived through the Great Depression and World War II, two events that forced Americans to become more resourceful due to difficult financial situations, food scarcity, and rations. People who consider themselves frugal are always looking for more ways to save money . To glean frugal wisdom from older generations that would still aply, one frugal person posed the question on Reddit: “What frugal lesson from your parents or grandparents you still use today?” Here are some of the best money-saving tips these Redditors picked up from their relatives: Reuse from your kitchen “My grandma rinsed and reused foil until it crumbled. I rolled my eyes then, now I catch myself doing it. Funny how those ‘silly’ habits end up smart. Mine also saves glass jars, labeled lids with tape, turned t-shirt into rags, and froze veg scraps for stock. :)” – YourxCherry “I save butter wrappers in the fridge to use for greasing baking pans. To get everything out of empty condiment bottles, I pour a little vinegar, milk or whatever is fitting, then shake it up and use that for salad dressing or other cooking needs.” – so-many-cats “I love Tostitos salsa jars. Whatever I cook, such as soup, ground beef, pasta, the extras, or leftovers, everything goes into these jars. They are so perfect for portioning. One jar = one person’s meal portion. I literally have more than 30 jars, and they are incredibly convenient!” – Proud_Possibility256 “I do not go grocery shopping until my fridge is empty including my freezer zero food waste. I have become very creative with recipes. Saves me money. Always take lunch to work.” – Samantha-the-mermaid “My grandmother took care of her five siblings during the depression after her parents died on .45¢ an hour. I make more money in an hour than she made in a week. She never wasted ANYTHING. She taught me to save bacon grease for seasoning, bread ends for bread pudding, leftovers for soup , and coffee grounds and eggshells for the garden. We didn’t carve our pumpkins- we painted them and made pumpkin pie out of it after Halloween.” – That-Response-1969 “I sometimes hate it that I am like this, but one of the first odd things that come to mind is labeling bottles of home goods like dish soap, body wash, bars of soap, hand soap, etc. so you know which one lasts the longest after purchase. Keep in mind, my grandmother grew up during the Great Depression. I also spent a majority of my days with her making food (predominately just standing around doing nothing useful). All of the meals we hold dear to our hearts are actually just frugal meals to stretch out. She would get extremely nervous if she came to your home and there were not canned goods. This is winter in the upper Midwest during the Great Depression to put it into perspective, along with canning and preparing for everything. This is a person that lived by candle light basically. When she finally had a icebox, every last meal had to be frozen. No matter what you made, it had to be able to sit there when necessary. You make no meal that cannot be eaten for three days or frozen solid for the next month. I still live by this routine.” – WideRoadDeadDeer95 Make your money go further “My mother taught me how to compare prices per item or ounce rather than by the package.” – Chicpea09 “My parents always framed purchases by how much time I would have to exchange for the item. So when I was in 6th grade and I wanted a TV for my bedroom and it was $120, I would have to do 6 to 10ish baby sitting jobs – then ask myself is it worth that exchange. This is still how I frame most purchases.” – BagNo349 “My grandfather told me as a teenager that debt is how other people control you. I didn’t realize how true this was until my early 20s when I got into mild debt problems. Since then I have been majorly debt averse.” – Egon88 “Mine told me if you cant pay the milkman 6pence this week, how will you pay him 12pence next week? Lesson learned. I pay my bills on time ALWAYS.” – Mundane_Sail_4155 “My dad always said it’s not a deal if you can’t afford it. Of course he didn’t have slickdeals either lol.” – JasonG5 “My grandpa always said ‘Pay yourself first.’ Even when money was tight, he’d stash $5–10 in savings before paying bills. I thought it was silly but that habit built a nice cushion over time.” – samdaz712 Save on utilities and living expenses “I hang dry my clothing whenever possible. I find it strangely relaxing to stand outside and carefully hang everything up so it has good airflow. It reminds me of helping my grandmother hang out laundry on their farm. The only thing I changed was painting the tips of my clothespins so I can see them better and don’t forget them on the line accidentally.” – SpecificSkunk “MAINTAIN and REPAIR what you already own. Lubricate, tighten, clean. Change filters. Replace belts. Flush. Air out. Condition. Resurface. Store properly. Take care of your stuff.” – i_know_tofu “I patch and repair clothes that can be repaired instead of immediately buying new. For instance, we have a comforter that has gotten holes from the washing machine – cheap materials. I’m learning the Japanese art of Shashiko to patch it over my Thanksgiving week break. I find a used item instead of buying new immediately, when our dryer went out, I bought one from an estate sale for the same price as repairing the old one would have cost (and since it was on it’s 3rd repair – heavy eye roll on cheaply made crap – I don’t feel so bad. I line dry a lot of things. Not everything but a lot.” – LeftwingSH “I put on hoodies and blankets and refuse to turn the heater on until the outside temps are about 45 degrees.” – thedoc617 “How to drive in order to maximize your miles per gallon and reduce wear and tear on the car. Accelerate slowly and try to keep under 2 RPMs. Leave a wide berth between yourself and other cars. Anticipate traffic/stopping, then let off the gas and cruise. Don’t ride the brakes.” – OrdinarySubstance491 What frugal lesson from your parents or grandparents you still use today? by u/YourxCherry in Frugal The wisdom holds up, all these years later There’s a reason these habits stuck around long after the Depression ended and the rationing stopped. They work. Not because they’re clever tricks, but because they reflect a fundamental shift in how you relate to the things you own, treating them as resources to be respected rather than conveniences to be used up and replaced. Our grandparents didn’t have the luxury of waste, and in learning from them, we might find that neither do we. The good news is that most of these tips cost nothing to start. Pick one, try it this week, and see what happens. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Frugal people share the best money-saving advice from parents and grandparents they still use appeared first on Upworthy .

Το αστείο είναι, σύμφωνα με έρευνες, αυτό δεν ισχύει στην πραγματικότητα. Μελέτες δείχνουν ότι το e…
items.descriptionOriginal: When we think of someone likable , we often imagine a person with a big personality who’s the life of the party. We conjure up images of social butterflies and people who keep everyone at the dinner party glued to their every word when they tell a story. The funny thing is, according to research, that’s not really the case . Studies show that the easiest way to make someone like you is to show interest by asking questions during the conversation and making it clear that you like them . People also really love those who come off as genuine. Michael Gendler, a co-founder of Ultraspeaking , a platform that helps people master the art of public speaking, shared three “magic” phrases on Instagram that make you more likable, all of which align with what science tells us. View this post on Instagram Three phrases that make you more likable 1: “Here’s what really scares me…” This phrase resonates with people because it shows you’re genuine by admitting your vulnerability. “Man, talk about your fears, real fears, not like ‘Oh, I’m scared I’m going to be too successful.’ Tell us about something that actually scares you. Don’t be guarded. Be open, and other people will appreciate that,” Gendler says. 2: “You know what I really like about you?” This phrase makes people like you because it counters a psychological phenomenon known as signal amplification bias, which suggests we tend to overestimate how clearly we express our feelings to others. This means that, many times, when we think others know we like them, they may not be so sure. So a little assurance goes a long way toward showing them the feeling is mutual. “People love being complimented as long as it is genuine,” Gendler says. 3: “Tell me more” As Dale Carnegie wrote in How to Win Friends and Influence People , the key to interacting with others is focusing on being interested in them rather than trying to impress them by being interesting. “To be interesting, be interested,” Carnegie writes. A Harvard study supports this, showing that people who ask more questions, especially follow-up questions , are better liked by their conversation partners. Redirecting the conversation back to yourself, on the other hand, tends to decrease liking. “People love feeling like what they’re saying is interesting. So invite them to speak more,” Gendler continues. Don’t forget to be genuine Ultraspeaking’s post is a breath of fresh air for those who aren’t comfortable trying to impress others at parties, on dates, or in the office. The video shows that if you make people feel important, they’re much more likely to like you in return. The key is that it has to come from the heart. “Remember, don’t just use these phrases and expect them to work,” Gendler says. “They have to be genuine and open. That’s what makes people likable.” This article originally appeared [time-difference] ago. It has been updated. The post Public speaking expert shares the 3 ‘magic’ phrases that instantly make you more likable appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: UPS drivers are always on the grind delivering packages around the clock, even on holidays. And one family took notice of the hard-working UPS driver in their neighborhood who had his nose to the grindstone as they enjoyed a cookout together. Rather than simply let him pass by, they decided to flag him down and extend an invite to join them in a move that proved community and hospitality are still alive and well. TikToker @1fanto shared a touching video with his followers from Easter weekend 2025 when his family invited a UPS driver making rounds in their neighborhood to come to their cookout and ‘make a plate.’ “Everybody family around here,” he captioned the video. “Everybody invited to the cookout.” @1fanto Everybody family around here ? #easter #cookout #wherethefunction ♬ original sound – Everything A1 There’s always room at this table In the video, the UPS driver is seen standing in the family’s driveway, and a group of cookout attendees warmly welcome him to join them. The uncle of @1fanto says to the driver, “You’ve been working hard all day man, you can go on in there!” He calls out for a woman named Stephanie to “take care of him!” The UPS driver walks up the driveway, and they encourage him to go inside and get his fill as he enters the garage. After securing a plate of food and a drink, the driver walks back outside to mingle with guests, shaking hands with the uncle who invited him. “You good?” the uncle asks, and the driver responds, “Yeah I’m good. They hooked me up. Thank you so much. Appreciate y’all for inviting me out.” On his way back to his truck, the uncle encourages the driver to invite other workers to stop by as well. How the invite really went down In a follow-up video, @1fanto explained more about how the invite went down. He shares that the UPS driver was driving by the family’s house on the Saturday before Easter, and at the time the family was enjoying a big fish fry cookout together. His uncle flagged the driver down, and he pulled over. He shares that his uncle told the driver, “Go inside and get you a plate!” The driver asked him, “Are you sure?” But he reassured him, adding that the family made sure to ask the driver what he wanted and didn’t want on his plate to “make sure he was good and got everything he needed”. “I saw it had a positive impact . That’s what my family do. That’s not something that we just do for social media,” @1fanto shared. “That’s something that we do on a regular basis that doesn’t just happen when the camera’s on. It happens when the camera’s off, too. We’re all equal. We all bleed the same.” Viewers were quick to show love Viewers had lots of positive things to say in the comment section. “I am a UPS driver and that makes our day. People showing love to us.” “Your family represents the best of America. Your uncle is now all of our uncle.” “Working the holidays suck. But they made that man’s entire day. Love it.” “I love when people are nice for no reason. You’re so real thank you for being so kind.” “Being a delivery driver is grueling, often thankless work. It’s awesome to see a family that remembers those hardworking folks are essential parts of our communities.” A little hospitality goes a long way Nothing about this invite was complicated. A family saw someone working through a holiday weekend, flagged him down, and made sure he left with a plate and a drink. As @1fanto put it, they do this when the camera’s off, too. Maybe the takeaway isn’t a grand gesture at all. It’s noticing the people who keep our neighborhoods running and making room for them at the table. The uncle even told the driver to invite his coworkers to stop by as well, because everybody’s invited. This article appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Family sees exhausted UPS driver working hard and invites him to ‘make a plate’ at family cookout appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Toddlers can be a handful, but they’re also the absolute best, with their tiny little adorableness, their burgeoning vocabulary , and their slowly evolving understanding of the world. Their imaginations are something else, and spending time in a wee one’s world is always an unpredictable treat. Being the parent of a toddler is a unique joy that only lasts for a fleeting season, so you have to take full advantage of it while you can. And one dad has clearly done just that. Christophe Kyle is father to Ava, who at 18 months old treated her dad to a meal at her sit-down restaurant. Only according to Kyle, the service left much to be desired. In a post on Instagram, Kyle shared a photo of Ava in her play kitchen while he sat waiting for his food in a tiny chair at a tiny table. View this post on Instagram Dad leaves a very honest review The father/customer wrote: “So I tried to support another Black Owned Business for lunch today. It’s called Ava’s Kitchen, just opened end of April. It’s a very clean establishment, but whewww let me tell you about this owner. First off, I asked why there are balloons on my chair, and it’s not my birthday? She talm’bout, mind yah business; those are Mommy’s. I been waiting on my order to get done for 45 minutes, and I’m the only customer here. She was making good progress at first, then she stopped for 20 minutes to go watch Paw Patrol. Overall the customer service could be better, but the cook is a cutie; so I’ll give her another chance. Let’s not give up on Black businesses so fast after one mistake.” The internet took a seat at the table People absolutely loved this dad’s humor and clearly stellar parenting skills. Anyone who has sat through a tea party, or any activity with the wee ones, knows that for all of its cuteness, toddler play is an exercise in patience and endurance. Upworthy shared Kyle’s story on our Instagram page and our readers did not disappoint. Some played right along with the game: “Starting a restaurant is tough.. give her a chance ” “I mean, she started a restaurant during a global pandemic, give her a break” View this post on Instagram “Is she taking reservations?” Fans of Paw Patrol had some words: “Paw Patrol is a must watch so “ “I died at Paw Patrol that’s my show though. I don’t have kids I just watch it just because lmao.” “Paw Patrol break is mandatory. Too cute! ” Others just gushed over the entire scene: “Love EVERYTHING about this!! The adorable owner, the customer’s humor and the incredible love.” “That’s the cutest restaurant owner I’ve ever seen. The dad’s face is priceless! ” “LoL the story is funny & beautiful!!! This warms my heart!! This babygirl will grow up to have such a healthy look at men (in any capacity) as long as she & her Daddy keep such a beautiful bond!! Happy Father’s Day (early) Keep encouraging her to do her thing and her confidence will continue to soar!! I just love this!!” What Ava and her dad did next Kyle soon followed up with a photo of a “line down the block” at Ava’s Kitchen, made up of stuffed animals. Since then, Ava and her dad have had some other creative adventures, including building things at Home Depot’s free monthly Kids Workshop: View this post on Instagram Will Ava be a restaurant owner, a carpenter, or something totally different when she grows up? Who knows, but with her dad’s support, no doubt she’ll build success wherever she ends up. This article originally appeared six years ago and has been updated. The post Dad shares ‘complaints’ about his toddler’s restaurant business and it’s too adorable appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: The Sydney Opera House, with its bold, innovative architecture, is said to be one of the world’s most photographed buildings — and it may soon share that status with another venue of its kind. Opening last week along China’s Huangpu River, the Shanghai Grand Opera House truly lives up to the adjective in its title. At nearly 1.6 million square feet, the performing arts center has three auditoriums seating 4,200 guests in total and will showcase everything from baroque opera and classical music to experimental productions. But what is perhaps its most awe-worthy attraction lies not within its walls but outside them: a stunning, spiral staircase that appears to be almost suspended in air. Yumeng Zhu The staircase connects the ground level to a rooftop observation deck that also serves as a stage, and visitors can access it regardless of whether they’re attending a show (cue the onslaught of social media selfies). Yumeng Zhu Restaurants, galleries, educational facilities, and other public spaces in and around the building are designed to welcome residents and tourists alike, positioning the opera house as a cultural landmark more than merely a ticketed institution. View this post on Instagram “People should be able to enjoy the building without attending a performance. It should become part of everyday life, a place to spend time, meet others, and experience the city,” Kjetil Thorsen, co-founder of Norway-based firm Snøhetta, which designed the building, told Dezeen. “A successful landmark is not only recognized by visitors, it is also embraced by the people who live around it and make it part of their everyday lives.” Snøhetta’s proposal won an international competition in 2016, and the firm teamed up with East China Architectural Design & Research Institute, Theatre Projects, and Nagata Acoustics in 2019 to bring the project from concept to completion. Wang Xiang—Xinhua/Getty Images The 2,000-seat main auditorium, called Harmony Hall, has five levels and three balconies. Soar Theatre, with a capacity of 1,200, is intended for more intimate productions, like operettas and plays, while the third auditorium, dubbed Open Stage, seats 1,000 and features adaptable stage and seating configurations, making it ideal for experimental works. The theme of movement was intentionally woven into the building’s architecture and aesthetic, a nod to the flowing river it sits adjacent to and the bustling city in which it’s located. Large glass windows let ample light in during the day and shift the mood for visitors as the sun sets or the weather changes. Tall outdoor towers are illuminated at night, marking the venue’s place within Shanghai’s skyline. Yumeng Zhu “A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of,” Thorsen told Dezeen. “When I last visited the site, I was asked by a Chinese architecture student how we managed to create a building that felt so Chinese despite not being from China. The answer lies in observation and understanding context.” RELATED: “First of Its Kind”: World’s Longest Outdoor Escalator Opens in China — Take a Virtual Ride

items.descriptionOriginal: When the documentary You Can See Everything unexpectedly smashed box office expectations with a massive $15 million opening, it got people talking. But it wasn’t just the film’s sheer shock value that had the internet buzzing. It was the teaser trailer released 40 days before the theatrical premiere that no one could initially look away from . The trailer featured lingering extreme close-ups of Elizabeth Holmes’ face that unsettled audiences everywhere. Viewers took to social media to share their sense of unease. But many couldn’t quite put their finger on why Holmes made them feel so off-kilter. Microexpression specialists are now breaking down the exact psychological triggers behind the viral reaction. The data reveal that our brains are responding to a deeply conflicting mix of emotions. Decoding the dissociative gaze The first piece of the puzzle lies in her eyes. On her Instagram , Facial Action Coding System (FACS)-certified expert Annie Sarnblad points to what she describes as a “dissociative gaze.” Psychologists have often referred to this involuntary defense mechanism as a “thousand-yard stare.” It typically communicates extreme stress and difficulty processing past traumatic events. View this post on Instagram When a person feels this level of extreme overwhelm, their mind may detach from the present moment. For the viewer, this blank, unblinking fixation triggers an innate survival warning. Sarnblad notes it “triggers our nervous system, putting us on high alert.” Yet, that vacant stare doesn’t exist in isolation. Paired directly with Holmes’ hollow eyes is her intentional, forced grin. Sarnblad compares it to the exaggerated smile of Batman’s arch-nemesis, the Joker. You may have also seen similar expressions used to unnerve audiences in Paramount Pictures commercial hits Smile and Smile 2 . The mask of a brave smile People can interpret an unblinking, detached gaze paired with an open smile in multiple ways. Sean Johns, a Body Language Expert with BodyLytics , shared his reaction to Holmes’ expression with Upworthy: “Her eyes and her smile are telling two different stories, and that’s why the clip gets under people’s skin.” Johns continued, “We make that face when something startles us.” She’s also trying to appeal to someone: take this in, please agree with me. The top half of her face says, ‘Please believe me.’ The bottom half, meanwhile, says that she’s fine.” Our brains struggle to reconcile the two contradictory expressions. A fascinating collision of human psychology This jarring emotional cocktail makes more sense, however, in context. The documentary was filmed inside Holmes’ personal residence, just four tense weeks before beginning her 10+ year prison sentence for corporate fraud. Sean Johns told Upworthy, “She wants this documentary crew to believe her. Holmes is weeks from prison, on camera, with someone openly doubting her—almost anyone’s face would be working this hard.” You Can See Everything offers a rare, complex look at how humans behave under extraordinary pressure, especially when they are desperate to be believed. For audiences, it’s a pivotal moment when pop culture and psychology collide. The post Microexpressions experts share the reasons why people find Elizabeth Holmes’ film clip so unsettling appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Socializing is an important part of life. It’s so important that people who prefer staying in rather than going out are often misunderstood. People who prefer to stay at home may be mistaken for being shy, introverted, or antisocial , but that’s not often the case. “Shyness is fear of social judgment, and a preference for quiet is simply a matter of where one gets energy from,” Nick Bach , Psy.D., HSPP, a licensed clinical psychologist and founder of Grace Psychological Services in Louisville, Kentucky, tells Upworthy. While some people feel energized by a night out, others feel drained. But that doesn’t mean they are lonely or in an unhealthy mental state. “What matters here is that someone has the option to choose solitude if they feel like doing so and have the opportunity to be part of their community and take advantage of activities and other social opportunities as well,” Dr. Robert Dean Davies, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist at Chroma Wellness Center , also tells Upworthy. Personality traits of people who prefer to stay home Psychologists and therapists share more about the personality traits of people who prefer staying in. Personality trait #1: They have strong self-awareness “People who want to stay at home probably know very well how they get energized,” says Dr. Davies. “They are aware of when being around people is enjoyable for them and when it is best to be alone. Recognizing when you need to decline an invitation to go out or do something can indicate that you understand yourself, not that you are socially uncomfortable.” Personality trait #2: They are practical “Practical people tend to make decisions based on facts, circumstances, and what makes the most sense instead of what sounds good in the moment,” Mary McLaughlin , LCSW, a psychotherapist in Vienna, Virginia, tells Upworthy. “They may consider the time and effort it takes to get ready, go out, and socialize and then decide that staying home feels like a better use of their energy.” Personality trait #3: They’re independent “Some people actually prefer being by themselves and do not have to be around other people all of the time to feel satisfied,” explains Dr. Davies. “They make decisions based on what makes them happy versus what will impress or please other people.” It also means they are emotionally independent. “Being comfortable when you are alone is indicative of your ability to be emotionally independent; it does not mean that you cannot relate to others,” adds Dr. Davies. Personality trait 4: They’re aware and conscious of their needs for energy “Those who do not wish to stay in know precisely what drains and recharges them,” says Bach. “They see that if they go out at night and there’s a lot of people, they use up their energy, but if there are no people there, they get it back. He adds that this is not avoidance, but rather emotional intelligence. “They have learned about their own nervous systems and respect them,” says Bach. Personality trait #5: They are thoughtful “Individuals who are at ease when alone will probably opt for those types of activities which foster an inner focus, i.e., reading, creating something, and/or having meaningful conversations,” Dr. Davies shares. “This preference for being alone can mean individuals require time to reflect on their own personal experiences without distraction. These preferences may also suggest these individuals have a more thoughtful approach toward life rather than indifference toward others.” Personality trait #6: They are structured “Structured people value routines and predictability. If going out disrupts their normal schedule, they’ll probably choose to stay in,” explains McLaughlin. She adds that while an invitation to go out on Saturday may sound fun to someone else, to them it may mean giving up the routine they look forward to. “For many people, routines aren’t just a preference. They provide a sense of stability and can help with emotional regulation,” she says. Personality trait 7: They’re selective, deep connectors People who prefer to stay in likely go deep in their relationships. “They prefer to invest their energy into a few strong friendships rather than a myriad of casual ones. If they do show up for someone, they are there and listening,” explains Bach. “Sometimes they would prefer to have one lengthy conversation with a close one rather than a night of conversation with a stranger. This typically means that they prefer depth over breadth in relationships.” Personality Trait 8: They are motivated from within “They do not require external validation, external stimulation, to feel full. Whether it’s a book, a hobby, cooking or time with family, their sense of a good evening comes from within,” Bach notes. “This can be a sign of a healthy sense of self, which is why they are not so driven by FOMO or ‘keeping up with the Joneses’.” The post Prefer staying in and saving energy over going out? Psychologists say you have these 8 traits. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Testing SEHMUA Infrared Solar Wildlife and Security Cameras Reading Time: 3 minutes The SEHMUA infrared solar wildlife and security camera pairs clean solar charging with invisible night vision to observe wildlife without disruption. The home security company SEHMUA recently sent Happy Eco News a two-pack of its 2K Solar Security Cameras Wireless Outdoor for review. My recent move to a rural property provided the ideal setting to test this sponsored package. SEHMUA offered me these cameras as a home security measure, but I live in a really safe area. Property crime is not really an issue here. I said yes because rather than record human intruders, my goal is to observe local wildlife cleanly, without running invasive power cords across the land. Living alongside nature means sharing boundary land with raccoons, black-tailed deer, and, a couple of times a month, mountain lions (cougars), as neighbors report. Using an infrared solar wildlife and security camera offers an easy way to secure my property while observing wildlife and other animals that may visit when I am not home. The SEHMUA IR night vision security cameras work for wildlife too. Licensed under the Unsplash+ License Each unit pairs with a detachable solar panel and an internal rechargeable battery. Sunlight powers the hardware continuously through daylight hours. As a result, users never need to haul heavy extension cords outside or take the gear down to recharge. Hardware setup takes about five minutes per unit on an exterior wall, tree post, or fence line. The wire-free design eliminates the need to drill through exterior frames or hire an electrician. The camera delivers 2K high-definition video. A 2K image contains double the clarity of standard 1080p high definition. This sharp resolution lets property owners verify distinct coat markings, antler points, or paw prints across the perimeter. A motorized lens rotates 355 degrees horizontally and tilts 90 degrees vertically to create a 360-degree panoramic view. One device can follow a foraging raccoon across a fence line that normally requires several fixed lenses. Each unit relies on a Passive Infrared sensor, known as a PIR sensor. A PIR sensor detects living body heat rather than blowing grass or swaying tree limbs. This heat-detection focus cuts out nuisance phone alerts while ensuring deer or cougars trigger instant recordings. The unit includes 500-lumen white spotlights and an intruder alarm for standard security deterrence. Obviously, when monitoring wildlife, sudden white light can startle shy animals and disrupt natural foraging habits. Switching the unit to infrared camera mode avoids this issue. Black-and-white infrared night vision uses invisible light beams to film nighttime visitors clearly up to 98 feet away without frightening them. This passive approach supports ethical wildlife observation. Homeowners can observe natural behaviors without feeding animals, baiting them, or disrupting their regular travel routes. Precise video timestamps also help map local wildlife activity patterns. Logging the exact arrival times of visiting deer, mountain lions, or raccoons reveals recurring habits. Knowing these schedules allows us to bring pets indoors well before large predators begin their evening hunt. Two-way audio allows owners to listen to ambient forest sounds directly through a smartphone. If an unwelcome predator (animal or human) approaches, I can manually trigger a 110-decibel siren. The hardware connects over standard 2.4 gigahertz Wi-Fi networks. It does not connect over 5 gigahertz bands. The manufacturer notes the camera operates reliably between minus 4 degrees and 122 degrees Fahrenheit. An IP65 weather rating protects the electronics against driving rain, snow, and wind. Footage saves directly to a local Micro SD card holding up to 128 gigabytes. This local storage setup avoids monthly cloud fees while saving hours of midnight animal visits. An optional cloud trial is also available for 30 days. Deploying an infrared solar wildlife and security camera gives rural residents peace of mind. Homeowners gain a non-invasive window into natural wildlife habits while safeguarding their homestead with clean solar energy. So far, I am impressed and will be doing a video review on the Happy Eco News YouTube channel in the coming weeks. The cameras are available through Amazon or directly from SEHMUA online. The post Testing SEHMUA Infrared Solar Wildlife and Security Cameras appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Buckwheat pillows offer a sustainable alternative to foam and polyester Reading Time: 3 minutes A farming byproduct that has filled pillows in Japan for generations is giving sleepers a plastic-free way to rest, and it can go back to the soil when it wears out. Every night, most of us rest our heads on a bag of plastic. Polyester fiber and memory foam, the two most common pillow fillings, are both made from fossil fuels. They clump, collect sweat and dust, and go flat within a year or two. Then the pillow gets thrown out. Most curbside recycling programs won’t take it, so it ends up in a landfill or an incinerator, and the cycle starts again with a new one. A growing number of sleepers are breaking that cycle with a leftover from buckwheat farming. A buckwheat pillow is filled with the hard outer shells of buckwheat seeds, the part nobody eats. Buckwheat is grown for its seeds, which are turned into flour, groats and noodles. Before the seed can be eaten, its tough, triangular shell has to be removed. Those shells, called hulls, are a byproduct of the milling process. Some are used for animal bedding or burned for fuel, but many have little value. Using hulls as pillow filling turns that waste stream into a useful product, in the same spirit as researchers turning leftover straw into crop waste fabric for clothing. No extra land is needed, because the hulls come from a crop that is already being grown for food. Pillows filled with buckwheat hulls have been used in Japan for generations, where they are known as sobakawa pillows. Their growing popularity in Europe and North America has more to do with materials: many shoppers now want a pillow that isn’t made from plastic. The crop itself also has a relatively light footprint. Buckwheat grows quickly, tolerates poor soils and generally needs little fertilizer. Its white flowers attract bees and other pollinators, and farmers often plant it as a cover crop to suppress weeds and protect the soil between other plantings. That doesn’t make every buckwheat pillow automatically green. Where the hulls are grown, how far they travel and how they are processed all make a difference. Hulls that are grown, milled and made into pillows in the same region carry far fewer transport emissions than those shipped across continents. No Fluff Pillow is one example of how short that supply chain can be. Its hulls come from a local buckwheat farm and are mechanically cleaned multiple times to remove dust and small particles. Each pillow is then filled by hand with 3.4 kg of hulls. Comfort is a big part of the appeal. Foam and polyester tend to trap heat, while hulls leave small air gaps between them so air keeps circulating. Many sleepers find that a buckwheat pillow stays noticeably cooler through the night. Buckwheat pillows also last much longer than conventional ones. Polyester fibers clump and foam gradually loses its shape, and neither can be repaired. Once they break down, the whole pillow has to be thrown away. Buckwheat hulls are hard and hold their shape for years. They slowly compress with use, and some break into smaller pieces, but owners can top the pillow up with fresh hulls or replace the filling entirely while keeping the same cover. Most buckwheat pillows also have a zipper, so sleepers can add or remove hulls to adjust height and firmness. One pillow can suit back, side and stomach sleepers, and a change in sleeping position doesn’t require a new purchase. When a buckwheat pillow finally does reach the end of its life, very little of it has to be thrown away. The hulls are plant material and can be added to a home compost pile or a yard waste bin, where they break down and return nutrients to the soil. Gardeners also use them as mulch. The cotton cover can be washed and reused, cut into cleaning cloths or taken to a textile collection point. A foam pillow, by contrast, has no practical recycling route in most places and can take decades to break down. Lawmakers are starting to take notice. California’s SB 707, the first statewide textile recycling law in the US, now covers pillows and bedding, and every EU country must set up similar producer-funded schemes for textiles by 2028. Buckwheat pillows do come with trade-offs. They are much heavier than fiber pillows, often weighing several kilograms. They are firm, molding to the head and neck rather than squashing flat, and most people need a few nights to adjust. They also rustle softly whenever the sleeper moves, a sound most people stop noticing within a week. Shoppers considering the switch can check where the hulls were grown and milled, how thoroughly they were cleaned, whether the cover is made from natural fibers such as organic cotton, and whether the pillow can be refilled rather than replaced. For households already composting food scraps or cutting back on plastic, the pillow is one of the easier swaps to make. The post Buckwheat pillows offer a sustainable alternative to foam and polyester appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Practical Bathroom Remodeling Ideas for a Safer, Sustainable, Easier-to-Maintain Home Reading Time: 4 minutes Practical Bathroom Remodeling Ideas for a Safer, Sustainable, Easier-to-Maintain Home Key Takeaways Plan around daily frustrations before choosing colors, tile, or fixtures. Prioritize safe shower access, reliable lighting, clear pathways, and moisture control. Select durable surfaces, simple fixtures, and storage that reduce routine cleaning and clutter. Consider household needs today while preparing for future changes in mobility needs. Build a budget that includes waterproofing, labor, permits, ventilation, and potential hidden repairs. A bathroom should support the way people actually live, from rushed weekday mornings to relaxed evening showers. A well-planned bathroom remodel can solve practical problems such as a high tub wall, poor lighting, cluttered counters, slippery flooring, or surfaces that require constant scrubbing. The best results come from treating the room as a connected system. Layout, drainage, ventilation, lighting, storage, and finishes all affect comfort, cleaning, and long-term performance. Start with the issues that make daily routines harder, then choose design details that support the solutions. Why Practical Planning Matters A remodel that looks appealing but ignores everyday inconveniences can become frustrating quickly. For example, a homeowner may love a decorative tile sample but discover that the new shower still has a difficult entry, no place to store toiletries, and dim lighting near the mirror. Addressing the function first makes it easier to select finishes that work with the room rather than against it. Inspect the Existing Bathroom Before demolition or shopping for products, inspect the room closely. Look for cracked tile, loose flooring, damaged caulk, water stains, soft walls, slow drains, peeling paint, and recurring mildew. Notice where water lands after a shower and whether the door, drawers, and cabinets open without blocking the walkway. Test switches, outlets, plumbing fixtures, and the exhaust fan. A fan that makes noise is not necessarily moving air outside effectively. Signs of plumbing leaks, electrical issues, extensive moisture damage, or a weakened subfloor should be evaluated by a qualified professional before selecting finishes. Set Clear Remodeling Priorities Separate your wish list into three categories so essential work remains protected if costs change: Must-haves: Repairs, waterproofing, safe entry, dependable lighting, and ventilation. Useful upgrades: Better storage, a handheld showerhead, seating, improved mirrors, and accessible controls. Optional details: Accent walls, premium hardware, decorative lighting, and smart features. Choose a Safer Shower Layout A standard bathtub, a tub-and-shower combination, a walk-in shower, a low-threshold shower, and a curbless shower can all be appropriate choices. The right option depends on the room’s size, plumbing arrangement, whether children use the bathroom, and the household’s current and future needs. For a shower-focused remodel, useful features can include accessible controls, a handheld showerhead, recessed niches, secure grab bars, and space to move near the entry. The home safety steps for preventing falls include brighter lighting, clear walking areas, and grab bars around tubs, showers, and toilets. Curbless showers can improve access, but they require careful attention to floor slope, drainage, waterproofing, and code-compliant installation. Improve Flooring and Lighting Bathroom flooring should be made for wet conditions and have a surface texture suited to areas that may become damp. Highly polished finishes can be harder to navigate when wet. Keep the route from the shower to towels and storage as short and uncluttered as possible, and use bath mats with stable, slip-resistant backing. Layered lighting makes routines easier. General ceiling lighting brightens the room; vanity lighting helps with grooming; shower lighting improves visibility in the bathing area; and low-level night lighting can make late-night trips more comfortable. Place switches where they are easy to reach when entering the room. Select Easier-to-Clean Materials Materials affect how much time a bathroom requires each week. Large-format tile can mean fewer grout lines than a small mosaic pattern, while smooth wall panels and nonporous counters can simplify wiping down wet areas. Simple faucet forms with fewer tight crevices are often easier to clean than highly detailed designs. Low-maintenance does not mean maintenance-free. Any shower wall, countertop, fixture, or floor still needs routine cleaning, sound installation, and prompt attention to damaged caulk or grout. Plan Storage Around Daily Routines Storage works best when it matches the items used every day. Keep frequently used toiletries between knee and shoulder height, use vanity drawers or pull-outs for small items, and place towels close to the shower or bath. Recessed niches can provide convenient shower storage when wall conditions allow. Medicines should be kept away from humid bathroom conditions, and reducing floor clutter can also reduce unnecessary bending and reaching. Control Moisture and Improve Ventilation Moisture can damage finishes and contribute to repeated mildew, condensation, musty odors, and peeling paint. An exhaust fan should vent outdoors rather than into an attic or another enclosed area. The EPA explains that bathroom ventilation removes unwanted moisture and recommends checking that the fan is functioning properly during renovation. Run the fan during bathing and afterward to help clear humid air. Also, inspect caulked joints, shower doors, and plumbing connections regularly, since small leaks are easier to address before they damage walls or flooring. Add Helpful Universal Design Features Universal design can look polished and inviting rather than clinical. Lever handles, handheld showerheads, comfortable fixture heights, wider clearances, seating, and contrast between controls and surrounding surfaces can support a wider range of users. If future grab bars may be helpful, plan wall reinforcement before the walls are closed. This small decision can make later updates simpler. Build a Realistic Budget and Remodeling Plan A complete budget should account for design, demolition, disposal, plumbing, electrical work, waterproofing, ventilation, flooring, wall finishes, lighting, fixtures, storage, permits, inspections, labor, and cleanup. Set aside a contingency amount for concealed leaks, damaged subfloors, or outdated plumbing that may be discovered after demolition. Compare detailed proposals rather than choosing only the lowest total. Then follow a clear sequence: List daily problems and measure the room. Choose must-haves before optional upgrades. Select the tub or shower layout. Coordinate lighting, ventilation, storage, and safety features. Review estimates, permits, scheduling, cleanup, and warranties. Test drainage, doors, drawers, lights, and fixtures during the final walkthrough. Common Bathroom Remodeling Questions Does a safer bathroom have to look clinical? No. Coordinated hardware, warm finishes, modern lighting, and built-in storage can make safety-minded features feel like a natural part of the design. Is a walk-in shower always better than a bathtub? No. A walk-in shower may improve access and reduce cleaning around a tub wall, while a bathtub can remain useful for children or household members who enjoy soaking. What should be checked at the final walkthrough? Confirm shower drainage and water flow, fixture stability, door and drawer clearance, switch placement, accessible storage, caulk details, cleanup quality, and warranty documents. Final Planning Tips Start with safety, moisture control, lighting, storage, and durable surfaces. Choose lasting features for the room’s permanent parts, then add personality with paint, mirrors, hardware, and accessories that are easier to change. A thoughtful plan can create a bathroom that looks finished, functions comfortably, and continues to support the household for years. The post Practical Bathroom Remodeling Ideas for a Safer, Sustainable, Easier-to-Maintain Home appeared first on Happy Eco News .
