items.descriptionOriginal: Every October, something beautiful begins to happen across Kashmir. The broad green leaves of the chinar trees slowly turn yellow. Soon, shades of orange and red begin to appear. By November, entire trees seem to glow in the autumn sunlight, their branches covered in leaves ranging from golden yellow to deep crimson. For Kashmiris, this is a familiar sign that winter is approaching. Known locally as boen or buen , the chinar ( Platanus orientalis ) is Jammu and Kashmir's state tree. Its enormous canopy provides shade through summer, while its changing colours have become one of the Valley's most recognisable autumn sights. But have you ever wondered why chinars turn such beautiful shades of red while so many trees in warmer parts of India stay green? The answer begins inside a single leaf. What happens to a leaf when winter approaches? Throughout spring and summer, chinar leaves are busy making food for the tree. Their green colour comes from chlorophyll, a natural substance that helps leaves absorb sunlight. Using this energy, the leaves turn water and carbon dioxide into sugars that help the tree grow. But as autumn arrives, Kashmir's days become shorter and temperatures begin to fall. The tree senses that winter is approaching and starts preparing for the colder months. Girls walk in a garden covered with fallen Chinar leaves during the autumn season in Kashmir https://t.co/byT5eUWu2C — Basit Zargar (باسط) (@basiitzargar) November 27, 2021 Before shedding its leaves, it draws back useful nutrients that can be stored and used again when spring arrives. As this happens, the green chlorophyll gradually breaks down. And something fascinating follows. Colours that were hidden beneath the green begin to appear. In their February 2011 Science Reporter article, Fiery Chinar , researchers Mohammad Imran Kozgar and Samiullah Khan explain how falling temperatures and declining chlorophyll reveal two groups of pigments called carotenes and xanthophylls. These are responsible for yellow and orange shades. In simple terms, the colours were already present in the leaves. The green was simply hiding them. But where does that beautiful red come from? Red leaves have another interesting story. In many trees that change colour during autumn, red and purple shades come from pigments called anthocyanins. Unlike the yellow and orange pigments, these can be produced as autumn progresses. Their formation is influenced by sunlight, temperature and the amount of sugar present in the leaves. However, scientists have not established exactly which pigments produce every shade of crimson seen in Kashmir's chinars. The 2011 article specifically explains the appearance of yellow and orange pigments. Kashmir's climate plays an important role in this seasonal transformation. Its broad canopy, distinctive leaves and striking autumn colours have made it a defining feature of the Valley's landscape. Photograph: (News18/Bashir Lone ; Getty Images) Chinars are deciduous trees, meaning they shed their leaves before winter. The Valley's shorter autumn days and falling temperatures help trigger this process. In warmer parts of India, many trees follow different seasonal patterns. Some remain green throughout the year, while others shed leaves during the dry season. For chinars, the changing colours mark a natural process of preparing for winter and conserving resources for the next growing season. Why Kashmir is working to save these trees The chinar's place in Kashmir extends far beyond its autumn colours. Mughal rulers planted these trees across the Valley, including at Srinagar's famous Naseem Bagh near Dal Lake. Their distinctive leaves continue to appear in Kashmiri embroidery, carpets and papier-m ch . But the trees have faced threats from damage, neglect and unauthorised cutting. In January 2025, The Indian Express reported on Jammu and Kashmir's Tree Aadhaar initiative, which gives individual chinars a unique identity to help authorities protect them. Project coordinator Dr Syed Tariq said that 28,560 trees had been geo-tagged at the time. Their records include location, age, size, health and possible threats, helping authorities keep track of individual trees. As Kashmir's chinars prepare to shed their leaves each winter, efforts to protect them carry a simple hope: that future generations will still be able to walk beneath their shade in summer and watch their leaves turn gold and crimson every autumn. Sources: 'Geo-tagging and 'Aadhaar': How, why the J&K govt is trying to conserve chinar trees' : Bashaarat Masood, Published on 26 January 2025 'Fiery Chinar' : By Mohd. Imran Kozgar and Samiullah Khan, Published in February 2011

items.description: Οι αστρονόμοι ανακάλυψαν τρεις μαύρες τρύπες που τροφοδοτούν ενεργά μέσα σε έναν μόνο γαλαξία που απέχει περισσότερο από 12,5 δισεκατομμύρια έτη φωτός μακριά, αποκαλύπτοντας μια αξιοσημείωτη σκηνή από τη βρεφική ηλικία του σύμπαντος. Δύο από τις μαύρες τρύπες χωρίζονται σε απόσταση μόλις 620 ετών φωτός και αναμένεται τελικά να συγχωνευθούν, ενώ μια τρίτη παραμονεύει πιο μακριά. Το ένα ζυγίζει εκπληκτικά 80 εκατομμύρια…
items.descriptionOriginal: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict.

items.title: Οι επιστήμονες ανακαλύπτουν πώς ο καρκίνος του παγκρέατος ξαναγράφει το DNA του για να ξεφύγει από τη θεραπεία
items.titleOriginal: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες ανακάλυψαν πώς τα καρκινικά κύτταρα του παγκρέατος αναδιαμορφώνουν συνεχώς τη γενετική τους σύνθεση για να γίνονται πιο επιθετικά, να εξαπλώνονται και να αποφεύγουν τη θεραπεία. Σε εργαστηριακά πειράματα, το μπλοκάρισμα ενός βασικού γονιδίου ανέστρεψε ορισμένες από αυτές τις επικίνδυνες αλλαγές, αποκαλύπτοντας έναν πιθανό νέο τρόπο καταπολέμησης της θανατηφόρας ασθένειας.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.

items.description: Ένα κοινό, φθηνό φάρμακο θα μπορούσε να περιέχει μια απροσδόκητη ένδειξη για την πρόληψη της άνοιας. Οι ερευνητές διαπίστωσαν ότι οι ηλικιωμένοι με συγκεκριμένο γενετικό προφίλ είχαν 70% χαμηλότερο σχετικό κίνδυνο άνοιας όταν έπαιρναν χαμηλή δόση ασπιρίνης, παρόλο που προηγούμενες μελέτες δεν βρήκαν συνολική προστατευτική δράση. Η ανακάλυψη υποδηλώνει ότι η γενετική θα μπορούσε να βοηθήσει στην εξήγηση του…
items.descriptionOriginal: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

Η γέφυρα, μήκους περίπου 630 μέτρων, συνδέει τη στεριά με το νησί και προσφέρει θέα στη λίμνη, στους καλαμιώνες και στις ορεινές πλαγιές που αγκαλιάζουν τον υδροβιότοπο. Καθώς απομακρύνεστε από την όχθη, το τοπίο ξεδιπλώνεται σταδιακά, με τα νερά και τη βλάστηση να αλλάζουν όψη ανάλογα με το φως. Στόχος είναι να περιοριστούν οι ακούσιες συσπάσεις της, οι οποίες προκαλούν αιφνίδια, έντονη ανάγκη για ούρηση και απώλεια ούρων. Όπως αναφέρει, η μέθοδος έχει λάβει έγκριση από τον αμερικανικό Οργανισμό Τροφίμων και Φαρμάκων (FDA) και εφαρμόζεται στις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες, στη Βρετανία, στη Γερμανία και στη Γαλλία. Ο ίδιος τοποθετεί την έγκρισή της περίπου ενάμιση χρόνο πριν και εκφράζει την προσδοκία ότι θα καταστεί σύντομα διαθέσιμη και στην Ελλάδα. items.descriptionOriginal: Η Ρίτα Αντωνοπούλου επιστρέφει με τη μουσικοθεατρική παράσταση «Της Γυναίκας σου η Καρδιά» στον Σταυρό του Νότου Plus, μετά τις παραστάσεις της άνοιξης του 2026 και την καλοκαιρινή περιοδεία σε πόλεις της Ελλάδας. Από την 1η Νοεμβρίου και κάθε Κυριακή στις 20:00, η καλλιτέχνιδα παρουσιάζει μια παράσταση που φέρνει τη μουσική σε διάλογο με τον θεατρικό λόγο, εξερευνώντας τη γυναικεία ταυτότητα σε όλες τις εκφάνσεις της. Με σύλληψη, κείμενα, σκηνοθεσία και ερμηνεία της ίδιας της Ρίτας Αντωνοπούλου, το έργο αναδεικνύει τις πολλαπλές πλευρές της γυναίκας: την κόρη, τη μητέρα, την ερωμένη και τη σύζυγο, αλλά και τη γυναίκα που αγαπά, αντέχει, διεκδικεί, συγκρούεται και αυτοσαρκάζεται. Πρόκειται για ρόλους που άλλοτε επιβάλλονται από την κοινωνία και άλλοτε αποτελούν προσωπικές επιλογές, διαμορφώνοντας μια σύνθετη εικόνα της γυναικείας εμπειρίας. Η μουσική συναντά τον θεατρικό λόγο Γνωστές και πρωτότυπες μελωδίες εναλλάσσονται με αφηγήσεις, δημιουργώντας έναν χώρο εξομολόγησης, όπου οι σιωπές, οι συγκρούσεις, το χιούμορ και η δύναμη της μεταμόρφωσης έχουν τον δικό τους ρόλο. Η χρήση τεχνητών μέσων, όπως χημικών, για ταχύτητα και αποτελεσματικότητα μπορεί εύκολα να καταστρέψει αυτά τα μικρόβια κάνοντας το έδαφος ξηρό, σκληρό και άψυχο. items.descriptionOriginal: Permaculture farmer Chau Quang Duong explains how the microbes that support life make up only 5% of the organic matter in living soil. Using artificial means, such as chemicals, for speed and efficiency can readily destroy those microbes making the soil dry, hard, and lifeless. In the same way, Chau cautions, when we give up our inner wisdom in total reliance on AI in the interest of speed, efficiency, and “perfection,” we risk destroying the living culture and knowledge of a local place from which life and our own inner wisdom grows – the 5% that AI can never provide. He suggests the need to continually replenish the soil of the soul through deep connection, such as immersion in a garden. “Just as the soil can recover when we stop damaging it and begin to care for it, our inner lives can become fertile again when we give ourselves time, space, and a deeper connection with nature.” “When the mind releases its need to control everything, a quiet, open space appears. In that space, our inner voice can begin to speak again.”

items.descriptionOriginal: A paintbrush moves slowly across the paper. Dhriti is focused on the colours in front of her, adding one shade after another to a painting that, to someone else, may simply look like a piece of art. But to her mother, Shweta Runwal, moments like these hold a much deeper meaning. Years ago, when Dhriti was still a little girl and could speak only in single words, she came home with a diary. On one of its pages, she had drawn two stick figures. One of them was crying. Shweta was worried and asked her daughter what had happened. Dhriti tried to explain that her friend was moving away. "It was the first time I realised she was actually trying to communicate through art," Shweta recalls. For a mother who had spent years hearing questions about what her daughter would or would not be able to do, the moment offered a different possibility. Perhaps the better question was not what Dhriti could not do, but what she could express, create and become. From paintings to lifestyle products, Tickle Your Art brings original artwork by neurodiverse artists to a wider audience while preserving the individuality of their work. That question would eventually grow into Tickle Your Art, a social enterprise that works with artists with Down syndrome and intellectual disabilities, turning their original artwork into lifestyle products, books, corporate gifts and more. But the idea did not begin as a business. It began at home, with Dhriti. Before the diagnosis, there was Dhriti Dhriti was diagnosed with Down syndrome a few days after she was born. At two months, doctors also discovered a hole in her heart and advised the family to consider surgery. For Shweta, the early years came with another challenge: the assumptions surrounding her daughter's diagnosis. "People saw her diagnosis before they saw her," she says. "They had already written her off." There were questions about whether Dhriti would walk or talk, whether she would ever have a career, and what her future would look like. At the time, Shweta says, there were fewer avenues for parents to find information or connect. Dhriti was Tickle Your Art's first artist. Today, the social enterprise has worked with more than 25 neurodiverse artists. Her own parents, however, took a different approach. "They were like, 'Just treat her like any other baby," she recalls. That trust became Shweta's biggest support system. She had trained as an architect and had also worked in London, where she first discovered how powerfully art and design could be used as forms of expression. But as Dhriti grew, Shweta began volunteering with the Down Syndrome Federation of India and meeting more families. She slowly began to notice a gap. The conversation was often about what children with intellectual disabilities might not be able to do. Shweta wanted to ask a different question: What if we started with what they could? Art became a language and a possibility After Dhriti's early experience with drawing, Shweta began looking for art classes for her. She eventually started working with several children, helping them explore different forms of creative expression. For Shweta, inclusion begins by looking beyond a diagnosis and recognising the creativity, skills and possibilities each person brings. In 2018, she organised an exhibition at Kelkar Museum around World Down Syndrome Day, bringing together artwork by people with Down syndrome and creating products around it. The response stayed with her. What began as a personal experiment eventually became Tickle Your Art, which was formally registered in October 2020, during the pandemic. Dhriti became its very first artist. Within six months, more artists began joining; today, Tickle Your Art has worked with more than 25 neurodiverse artists and is onboarding six more for upcoming launches. The organisation also runs a community centre where artists receive training, mentorship and employment opportunities, alongside an experience centre where visitors can encounter their work and the stories behind it. Importantly, the artists do not have to fit into a predetermined idea of what "good" art should look like. "We try not to change the artwork as much as possible," says Shweta. "We want to see their story." Dhriti's artwork was first showcased at an exhibition organised by Shweta at Kelkar Museum in 2018. Sometimes, that means designing around an artist's original lines or colours. Sometimes, it means finding a new way to translate their work into a product. Every product carries the story of its artist. Shweta describes the idea simply: each product should be responsible for "three smiles" — that of the artist, the person giving it and the person receiving it. At home, inclusion came naturally For Ira, Shweta's younger daughter, this entire world has always been normal. "I've never felt this is very different," Ira says. "I've never thought about inclusion, because it is normal for me, and that's how it should be for everyone." That belief has grown alongside the enterprise. Today, Ira contributes to Tickle Your Art's marketing and design decisions. Shweta jokes that nothing goes into production without Ira's approval. Ira can look at a product and instinctively understand what might appeal to someone, where something should be placed, or how a design could work better. Ira Runwal contributes to Tickle Your Art's marketing and design, believing inclusion should be a natural part of everyday life. But her role goes beyond the business. She also speaks about inclusion in schools and has received recognition for doing so. For Shweta, watching her daughters grow up together has reinforced something she has long believed: inclusion does not have to be complicated. "It doesn't belong to anybody," she says. "Just give a smile, and others will smile back at you." When talent finds a place to work For Shweta, economic inclusion is not simply about giving someone a job. It is about helping them recognise that their time, talent and contribution have value. She remembers when Rohan, a 33-year-old artist with a background in animation and digital design, began working with Tickle Your Art. When Shweta started paying him, his father wondered whether the small organisation should really be giving him a salary. For Shweta, there was no question."He is giving his time. He is coming here sincerely. And I feel that needs to add value," she says. That philosophy is also reflected in the way Tickle Your Art operates. Artists can work from home or at the centre, and their work is developed into products based on its originality and the story behind it. The organisation has now worked with artists across India, with many connections coming through disability organisations and communities. At Tickle Your Art, Rohan has found an opportunity to reconnect with his passion for art and rebuild his confidence through meaningful work. For Suzanne, who brings around three decades of HR experience and works with Tickle Your Art as an HR consultant, this has also changed the way she understands inclusion. "In corporate, we talk about diversity, equity and inclusion," she says. "But very rarely do we get to live it the way Shweta is living it." Her role is largely focused on building the systems and processes that allow the organisation to function sustainably, while Shweta works closely with the artists and creative side. Suzanne says she has also noticed something else: people sometimes hesitate because they do not know how to interact with people with intellectual disabilities. "But I have found Dhriti to be extremely loving, warm, intelligent and funny," she says. "They are just like you and I. There's no difference." When confidence finds its way back Before Tickle Your Art, 33-year-old Rohan had already worked in animation and had trained in Photoshop, Illustrator and other digital tools. But after his earlier job ended during the lockdown, he became more introverted. Then came Tickle Your Art; Rohan has now been associated with the organisation for around a year. His mother, Veena, says art has always been one of his biggest interests. At Tickle Your Art, however, she has watched that interest become a source of confidence and happiness again. Tickle Your Art develops products around artists' original creations, ensuring their distinctive styles and stories remain at the heart of the process. For Veena, that happiness is perhaps the most meaningful change. She has also seen how spaces like Tickle Your Art can shift the conversation for families, giving children opportunities to learn, work and meet people outside their homes. And that, ultimately, is what Shweta wants to build. A space that feels like home Tickle Your Art has received recognition from several platforms, including Shark Tank India, where Anupam Mittal invested in the venture. It has also received grant support from Jeet Adani, been recognised as an "Industry Disruptor" by UN Women, and showcased its work internationally in Berlin at The DO and H&M exhibition. Dhriti, meanwhile, received the National Award for Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities in the Shreshth Divyang Balika category for her achievements in art and her role in promoting inclusion. For Shweta, these milestones matter, but not simply because they validate the organisation. She remembers a parent of a six-month-old child with Down syndrome reaching out after seeing Dhriti's videos. The mother told her that she had felt shattered after the diagnosis, but seeing Dhriti had given her hope. "That is what makes me feel that all of this is worth it," Shweta says. Dhriti received the National Award for her achievements in art and contribution to promoting inclusion. Her dream now is to build similar community spaces across India, places where families can come together, where artists can learn and work, and where art can become a bridge to meaningful livelihoods. Ira imagines Tickle Your Art becoming known across India and eventually the world. Shweta has an even simpler measure of success: working with many more artists and giving them a platform to begin. For her, the centre should feel like a second home. A place where a person's diagnosis does not decide their possibilities, where a painting is not treated as something made "despite" a disability, but simply as someone's art. And perhaps, most importantly, a place where inclusion stops being a lofty idea and becomes what Ira has always known it to be — normal. All images courtesy of Shweta Runwal

items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.

items.descriptionOriginal: Saul Levmore and Ward Farnsworth are college professors, so it’s fitting that the title of their new book is a question rather than an answer (beyond that being a fair way to pique interest). Like all good teachers, the authors don’t just want us to learn — they want us to learn how to think . In Should You Tip for Takeout? , they mine the fields of law, economics, philosophy, sports, and rhetoric to present a “tool kit for a more rational life.” Far from being an etiquette guide, it’s instead an invitation to expand the way we look at the world, so we can better understand not only our own behavior but others’ as well. Each chapter uses a common quandary — like whether you should recline your airplane seat or get a second opinion before surgery — as a jumping-off point to introduce heuristics and critical thinking techniques that can be applied to countless other scenarios. The resulting pages offer up food for thought and fodder for lighthearted debates. “One way to think about it is we’re trying to write a book that helps people have more fun having conversations at the dinner table,” Farnsworth explained in an interview with Nice News, noting that discussions these days seem to so easily devolve into political arguments or fear-based speculations about the future. “We thought, ‘You know, there’s a lot of things just in everyday life that are actually pretty interesting to think about if you look more closely at them than most people usually do,’” he said, adding: “What would it mean to really take this one apart rationally? What can you learn about the problem that makes everyday life a little more interesting, and maybe what can you learn about rationality that makes other things easier to understand?” Again, anyone hoping for simple “yes” or “no” solutions to life’s dilemmas would be opening the wrong book. In a chapter called “Should You Keep Looking for a Better Price?,” for example, the authors encourage readers to acquaint themselves with distribution patterns and standard deviations. In another, they demonstrate how one might use the mathematical theory of optimal stopping to choose a romantic partner. (Essentially: View the first 37% of your dates or relationships as a comparison pool, and then pick the first subsequent person who’s better than the best one in the sample cohort.) Photo by Lloyd DeGrane from UChicago Saul Levmore That’s not to say there are no straightforward answers. The title chapter delves into the power we have with our wallets to vote for or against a custom when it hasn’t yet become a norm. If something has become entrenched, it’s likely in our best interest to go along with it, whether or not we agree. In the case of tipping for takeout, the authors say that the verdict is in: It’s the norm, so you should tip what you deem a reasonable amount. And doing so may not matter as much to your pocket as you might imagine. “Think of it as a hidden price hike,” Farnsworth said. “But the good news is that you have something to say about it. You have some discretion on how much you’re going to let that price go up. And that should be considered a welcome thing rather than a bad thing, because the alternative is the price goes up for everybody.” The authors said that simply musing through these kinds of common scenarios can reveal possibilities one may never have considered for why things are the way they are and what alternatives exist. Courtesy of Godine Ward Farnsworth “One broad takeaway to me is that people should experiment more in their own lives,” Levmore said, adding, “I think the book tries to encourage people to imagine how the world could be a little bit different from the way it is.” It may also help expand our empathy, Farnsworth pointed out. “Sometimes looking at life and looking for the rationality in it is a way to be more generous-minded toward other people who appear to just be annoying you at random and may be doing just what you would do if you were in their shoes.” When our conversation turned to the most favorable order in which to be interviewed for a job, the pair demonstrated — perhaps unintentionally — just how the aforementioned dinner table discourse may go. “I think it’s a disadvantage to be the last person,” Levmore said, prompting Farnsworth to disagree: “I generally think you want to go last. You want to go as late as you can.” “They get tired,” Levmore rejoined after Farnsworth elaborated, to which Farnsworth replied, “Maybe,” then added: “There’s no right answer to these questions. We just think these problems that most of us sort of wander through unconsciously, they’re just more interesting when you slow down and really ask, ‘What is the best way to handle this?’”

items.description: Γνωρίζατε ότι σε μια ινδική πολιτεία, οι γυναίκες διαχειρίζονται επιχειρήσεις, κυκλοφορούν πιο ελεύθερα και περπατούν στο σπίτι τη νύχτα με μεγαλύτερη αυτοπεποίθηση; Η Mizoram προσφέρει μια ενδιαφέρουσα προοπτική για το πώς η δημόσια συμμετοχή των γυναικών, η οικονομική ανεξαρτησία και η καθημερινή κινητικότητα μπορούν να διαμορφώσουν τις κοινωνικές προσδοκίες. Από τα αγόρια που μαθαίνουν τις οικιακές ευθύνες μέχρι τις γυναίκες…
items.descriptionOriginal: Did you know that in one Indian state, women run businesses, move around more freely, and walk home at night with greater confidence ? Mizoram offers an interesting perspective on how women’s public participation, economic independence and everyday mobility can shape social expectations. From boys learning household responsibilities to women participating in markets and community life, the idea goes beyond individual empowerment. It challenges traditional gender roles and highlights how equality can begin at home, through the habits children learn and the responsibilities families share. What can the rest of India learn from Mizoram about women’s safety, gender equality and women’s freedom? This story explores why building a more equal society requires more than asking women to be careful. It requires everyone to play a part. #Mizoram #GenderEquality #WomensSafety #EqualityBeginsAtHome #GenderEqualityInIndia #RaisingBoys #WomenEmpowerment #MatrilinealSociety #NortheastIndia #thebetterindia Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.titleOriginal: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
items.description: Μια μικρή συσκευή που διεγείρει απαλά τα νεύρα μέσω του αυτιού θα μπορούσε να προσφέρει έναν νέο τρόπο για την αντιμετώπιση της επίμονης υψηλής αρτηριακής πίεσης. Σε μια κλινική δοκιμή 63 ασθενών που έπαιρναν ήδη φάρμακα, η θεραπεία αποδείχθηκε ασφαλής, εύκολη στη χρήση στο σπίτι και καλά ανεκτή. Αν και δεν ξεπέρασε σημαντικά το εικονικό φάρμακο συνολικά, οι ασθενείς με πιο σοβαρή υπέρταση…
items.descriptionOriginal: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure.

items.description: Μια μεγάλη μελέτη αποκάλυψε κρυμμένα προειδοποιητικά σημάδια φλεγμονώδους νόσου του εντέρου στο αίμα έως και 10 χρόνια πριν από τη διάγνωση. Οι ερευνητές ανακάλυψαν διαφορετικά μοτίβα αντισωμάτων που θα μπορούσαν να βοηθήσουν στην πρόβλεψη του ποιος θα αναπτύξει αργότερα τη νόσο του Crohn ή την ελκώδη κολίτιδα, ξεχωρίζοντας ακόμη και τα άτομα που διατρέχουν κίνδυνο πιο περίπλοκης νόσου.
items.descriptionOriginal: A major study has uncovered hidden warning signs of inflammatory bowel disease in the blood up to 10 years before diagnosis. Researchers discovered distinct antibody patterns that could help predict who would later develop Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, even distinguishing people at risk of more complicated disease.

Η ανακάλυψη βασίζεται σε πειράματα σε ποντίκια που έδειξαν αξιοσημείωτη αντίσταση στην παχυσαρκία και βελτιωμένη μυϊκή αντοχή, αυξάνοντας τις ελπίδες για μια νέα προσέγγιση στη θεραπεία απώλειας βάρους.
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have discovered that switching off a protein called Mitch makes human cells burn more fat and prevents new fat cells from developing. The breakthrough builds on experiments in mice that showed remarkable resistance to obesity and improved muscular endurance, raising hopes for a new approach to weight-loss treatment.

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία είναι μέρος της σειράς "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's υπό την ηγεσία των ανθρώπων της σειράς γονέων που ξεπερνά τις συμβατικές συμβουλές για να τεκμηριώσει πώς οι πραγματικές οικογένειες μεγαλώνουν πραγματικά τα παιδιά τους. Μέσω πραγματικών γονέων, προπονητών γονέων, επιρροών και ειδικών, η σειρά φέρνει ειλικρινείς, διαφορετικές και σχετικές προοπτικές για το q…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "Parenting: What Google Won't Tell You" — The Better India's people-led parenting series that goes beyond conventional advice to document how real families are actually raising their children. Through real parents, parenting coaches, influencers and experts, the series brings honest, diverse and relatable perspectives on the questions, choices, challenges and solutions that shape everyday parenting — the things Google can't always answer. When Aayansh Singh first visited a farm near Mumbai, the horses, pigs and hens he had seen in picture books suddenly had a life of their own. Two years later, he returned with one wish: to ride a horse. For his father, Bhanu Singh, a software engineer based in Mumbai, watching that wish come true was a reminder of how much a child can take away from an experience that seems simple to an adult. "When we first took him, I honestly thought he would forget everything because he was only two years old," Bhanu recalls. "But for the next year, he kept talking about the horses and remembering the farm." It began with a small observation at home. Aayansh, then two, could identify horses, pigs, cows and goats from his picture books. He knew what they looked like, but he had never encountered them outside the pages. What began as a day of discovery became a memory Aayansh continued to talk about long after returning home. "We wanted him to go beyond books and experience them firsthand, to see them up close, touch them, and understand how they feel and behave," Bhanu says. That thought led the family to Japalouppe, a farm they discovered while searching online for a place near Mumbai where their toddler could meet animals. When the pictures came alive The family kept their first outing simple. Japalouppe was about a 1.5-hour drive away, making it manageable for a day trip with a young child . There was no packed itinerary or long list of attractions to tick off. For Bhanu Singh, the experience was a reminder that simple outings can leave lasting impressions on young children. Bhanu was drawn to the farm's open spaces, animals and horses. They also carried some food, unsure whether they would find suitable, non-spicy options for Aayansh. To their pleasant surprise, the farm had a child-friendly menu. Once they arrived, the family let the day unfold at Aayansh's pace. "He didn't run around shouting or get overwhelmed. He was quiet, curious, and busy taking everything in," Bhanu remembers. One moment that stayed with him was watching his son run around the hens. Until then, hens had been pictures in a book. Now, they were moving around him, clucking and going about their business. The horses and pigs offered another kind of discovery. "He looked at the horse like he was thinking, 'This is the horse from my book.' He did the same with the pig. In his book, it was just a picture, but here it had a smell and made a sound. For him, it was a big thing." The family's two visits showed how hands-on experiences can help children build on what they learn from books. For the adults, these might have been ordinary sights and sounds. For Aayansh, they were details that no picture could quite capture. The family stayed close, letting him decide how near he wanted to get to each animal. A dedicated guide showed them how to approach and handle the animals safely, explaining which feed to offer and how to do it. There was no need to hurry him along. If something caught his attention, he could stay and watch. From watching horses to riding one The first visit was about getting acquainted with the animals. Aayansh was too young to ride a horse, but the experience left him with memories he continued to talk about long after the family returned home. Then, at three and a half, he asked to visit the farm again; this time, he had a plan of his own. "He clearly told us he wanted to visit again and ride a horse," Bhanu says. At three and a half, Aayansh returned to the farm with a wish of his own: to ride a horse. The family returned, and Aayansh got his wish. He was the youngest child on the farm to ride a horse that day, making the moment especially memorable for his parents. Bhanu noticed how much had changed. On the first visit, his son had watched the animals with wide-eyed curiosity. Now, he knew what he wanted to do. He approached the experience with greater confidence , going around to meet the animals again, almost as if he were reconnecting with old friends. "For us, the most special part was watching him sit on the horse with so much pride," Bhanu says. "The first trip was about discovery, while the second was about building on those memories and trying something new on his own." A holiday doesn't need a packed itinerary The two visits changed the way Bhanu thinks about family holidays. Earlier, he associated a good holiday with travelling to a new destination and having plenty of activities planned. Now, he finds himself asking a different question before choosing a place: "What will my child actually experience here? What will he see, feel, and remember?" His advice to parents who want to introduce young children to nature is to start small. Choose a place close to home, perhaps somewhere connected to an animal or activity the child already loves, and leave room for curiosity to lead the way. "Don't try to fit too many activities into one day. Let your child explore at their own pace, follow their curiosity, and enjoy the little moments," he says. After all, Aayansh's first farm visit wasn't filled with elaborate attractions or a faraway holiday backdrop. It was a day of watching hens, meeting pigs and standing close to horses he had previously known only from books. For parents, Aayansh's story is a reminder that meaningful family holidays need not involve packed itineraries or faraway destinations. Yet those encounters stayed with him. They even gave him something to look forward to when the family returned. And perhaps that's one of the loveliest things about travelling with children: you may plan the outing, pack the snacks and choose the destination, but you never quite know which small moment will find a permanent place in their hearts. And sometimes, the best souvenirs from a family holiday are the memories a child carries home, and the little adventures they can't wait to have next. All images courtesy of Bhanu Singh

items.descriptionOriginal: Cut open a ripe jackfruit, and you are greeted by its golden-yellow flesh, sweet aroma and sticky, fibrous peel. While the juicy fruit often finds its way into curries, chips and desserts, its thick outer covering usually ends up in the bin. Researchers at the National Institute of Technology (NIT) Rourkela , however, have found another use for this often-discarded part of the fruit. They have turned jackfruit peel into a material that removed more than 90% of fluoride from contaminated water in laboratory tests, in about 10 minutes. The idea brings together two things that rarely make it into the same conversation: fruit waste and safer drinking water. For families whose groundwater contains too much fluoride, which can damage teeth and bones over time, this innovation could eventually offer a more affordable way to make drinking water safer. How does jackfruit peel help clean water? The secret lies in what researchers have made from the peel. The team converted discarded jackfruit peel into activated carbon and modified it with zirconium, a metal that helps the material capture fluoride from water. Modified with zirconium, jackfruit-peel-based activated carbon helps capture excess fluoride from contaminated water. Photograph: ( Nature ) Prof. Susmita Mishra, Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering at NIT Rourkela, explains the thinking behind the innovation. "The key idea behind this technology is to use an agricultural waste material as a resource for water purification. We prepared activated carbon from discarded jackfruit peel and modified it with zirconium to improve its ability to capture fluoride from water," she adds. The material showed promising results in laboratory tests, removing over 90% of fluoride within approximately 10 minutes under the tested conditions. Fluoride occurs naturally in water, but drinking water containing too much of it over a long period can damage teeth and bones. This condition, known as fluorosis, can affect both children and adults. Removing excess fluoride, however, is not always straightforward. Reverse osmosis, a widely used water treatment method, can waste considerable amounts of water and remove minerals such as calcium and magnesium. Other methods, including ion exchange and activated alumina, also come with limitations, including the use of chemicals that can raise environmental concerns. The NIT Rourkela team's approach explores whether an agricultural by-product can help make fluoride removal more accessible. What did the researchers find? In laboratory experiments, the jackfruit-peel-based material removed more than 90% of fluoride from water containing around 1–5 milligrams per litre. Under the tested conditions, the team recorded removal efficiencies of over 90–97% within 10–20 minutes. The patented innovation by NIT Rourkela researchers offers a new approach to tackling fluoride contamination using agricultural waste. Photograph: ( Gujarat Samachar ) The researchers have also secured a patent for the technology. The team comprises Prof. Mishra and Dr. Pratima Minz, Research Graduate at NIT Rourkela. They estimate that preparing the material costs approximately Rs 37 per gram, based on the electricity and chemicals used in its synthesis. These are promising early findings, but there is still some way to go before the material can be used to treat drinking water outside the laboratory. The research has reached Technology Readiness Level 4 (TRL 4), meaning the material and its underlying concept have been validated in a laboratory environment. What happens next? For families in rural and semi-urban areas where groundwater contains excess fluoride, an affordable treatment option could make a meaningful difference. The researchers hope their material could eventually be used in decentralised water treatment systems, bringing purification closer to the communities that need it. Prof. Mishra says, "The potential of this technology lies in its use of an easily available agricultural by-product to develop a cost-effective material for fluoride removal. In the long term, the technology could contribute to water treatment solutions for communities in fluoride-affected regions, subject to further testing and validation." The team is now working towards a prototype to test the material's potential beyond the laboratory. Photograph: ( The Printlines ) The next step is to develop a physical prototype and test how the material performs in practical conditions. The team will also study its long-term performance and operating costs to understand whether it can be deployed on a larger scale. A discarded jackfruit peel is not yet ready to make drinking water safer on its own. But this research offers an interesting possibility: something routinely thrown away could, with further development, become part of a solution to a problem that affects communities across India.

items.descriptionOriginal: A 50-year-old Japanese planting method is quietly reshaping vacant lots, schoolyards, and parking strips across the United States -- not through large-scale industrial effort, but through the hands of neighbors who show up on a Saturday to tuck seedlings into carefully prepared soil. Developed by botanist Akira Miyawaki, the method skips the slow prologue of natural forest succession, mixing climax species and their supporting plants to create self-sustaining ecosystems within decades rather than centuries. What makes it remarkable is not just the science but the ritual embedded in it: "He would take each plant, and the community had to say its name," recalls one organizer -- "it was about restoring relationships between humans and non-humans." The miniforest movement asks something modest of each participant and returns something harder to name: a sense of belonging to a place, and a stake in its future.

items.descriptionOriginal: At Bengaluru's Racecourse Junction, people crossing the road had to spend longer than necessary among moving vehicles. One turn gave cars a generous sweep of the road, leaving pedestrians to find their way through traffic. When urban designers Nishita Parmar and Vedanti Agarwal studied the junction, they discovered something surprising. Relatively few vehicles were using one left turn, while far more people needed to cross that stretch. Why, then, was so much space being given to cars? Working with principal designer Monik Shah and the team at Compartment S4 , they helped redesign the junction to include a pedestrian refuge island, giving people somewhere to pause while crossing. The work was part of the Orbital project, commissioned by the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) and supported by the Sustainable Mobility Network. It was one example of a question guiding their work across Bengaluru: how can streets and the spaces around them better serve people on foot? Why did one left turn have so much space? The team began at Racecourse by observing how people and vehicles actually moved. They counted traffic, followed pedestrian routes and noted where the two came into conflict. "When we actually went and mapped that entire junction, we understood that the volume of vehicles coming from [the road] and going towards the left was much lower compared to the volume of pedestrians," Parmar says. That meant pedestrians were crossing a wider stretch of moving traffic than necessary. "We call it pedestrian exposure time. To cross from A to B, it took a longer time, and that means you're getting exposed to the moving vehicle for longer," she explains. The designers proposed a more compact turn, changes to traffic movement and a refuge island to break up the crossing. For someone walking to college, work or another destination, spending less time among vehicles could make the journey easier. This matters at a junction serving the Race Course, educational institutions and other destinations. Students and other pedestrians pass through daily, while events bring larger groups into the area. At Racecourse Junction, vehicles had a generous sweep of the carriageway to negotiate one of the turns. Photograph: Atik bheda By December 2023, BBMP had begun redevelopment work at Race Course Road junction, including plans for pedestrian crossings, seating and waiting areas. In February 2025, local reporting described the redevelopment as completed, with benches installed for pedestrians and officegoers . Compartment S4 also lists its Race Course Junction project as completed. A road can appear to need more space for vehicles because of the way it has been designed. But once actual movement is measured, the hierarchy can look different. Photograph: Atik bheda The physical intervention is documented, although published before-and-after figures showing reduced crossing times or traffic conflicts were not available for this story. Why test a design on the street first? Parmar trained as an architect at CEPT Ahmedabad. Her experience in urban design and strategy, including work with Jaipur's Domestic Workers' Union, exposed her to the ways public infrastructure affects everyday lives. Agarwal, who has a Master's in Urban Design from UC Berkeley, has worked on urban mapping, landscape-led planning, transit-oriented development and environmentally sensitive design in India and the United States, including at WRT's San Francisco studio and Studio POD in India. Their approach begins with observing rather than assuming. Before committing to permanent changes, the team tested how a redesign worked on the street. That matters because people rarely move exactly as a drawing predicts. Someone may take a shortcut across the road; a driver may turn differently when traffic builds up. Watching these movements allows designers to identify problems and adjust plans before construction becomes permanent. "The issues never come under one sort of bucket. There is a transport issue, there is a utility issue, there is a space-constraint issue, there is a traffic issue, and everything comes together to form an urban issue," Parmar says. They began looking for locations where one intervention could address several concerns, including awkward road edges and spaces left beneath flyovers. "We started mapping these areas or these locations where there is some kind of demonstration possible to make that a lighthouse project and show how you can think of spaces, otherwise negative spaces or deformed spaces in the city, as something different," she says. Turning such ideas into actual spaces also means working within government approvals, budgets and construction constraints. "If we aim for something really high in the first go, it might not get passed or it might not have the budgets to get implemented," Parmar explains. "Whatever intervention we do, it is not only solving one particular thing, but it is looking at all the aspects of issues in an urban context," she adds. That thinking led the team to Shivananda Flyover. Turning unused flyover space into a public park At Shivananda, a large area beneath the flyover was going unused, while people passing through had barely 1.5 feet of footpath to walk on. The team's surveys showed that pedestrians were already using this route between residential neighbourhoods, universities and the Race Course. The designers wondered whether some of the underused land could become a more welcoming place for them. "The flyover was taking up a lot of space which was unused," Parmar says. "So we thought, let's take this and integrate it with the junction." Their response was Pause Park, designed with seating, platforms, steps, swings, greenery and art. The aim was to give people a place to sit and spend time in an area they previously had little reason to stop in. The area connects residential neighbourhoods with universities and the Racecourse, meaning people were already using it as part of their daily routes. Photograph: Archana Venson Work to make the area useful was under way by June 2023, when BBMP was constructing benches and public toilets after residents objected to an earlier proposal for a basketball court and skating rink, citing safety concerns around nearby traffic . In February 2025, civic officials described Shivananda Circle among junctions they had developed. However, a report on 31 May 2025 said finishing work on the mini park's swings and greenery was still in its final stages. An exact public opening date, and whether all facilities are currently accessible, could not be independently confirmed. The idea nevertheless poses a valuable question for a city full of flyovers: could the land beneath them offer something useful to the people who walk past every day? Will people actually use these spaces? For road junctions, the team can examine crossing times, traffic flow and potential conflicts between pedestrians and vehicles. "For junctions, it is about seeing how smooth the traffic flow has become. These things are more objective," Agarwal says. The team is also examining how urban design might lessen the effects of heat. After a space is built, they consider post-occupancy studies , returning to see how people actually use it. "For open spaces, it is about going during the most active hour and seeing whether the community has adopted it," Agarwal says. The resulting Pause Park introduces seating, platforms, steps, swings, greenery and art into the space beneath the flyover. Photograph: Archana Venson Are children playing there? Are older people sitting comfortably? Can different groups share the space? Such observations help show whether a public place is working as intended, and what may need to change. What it takes to get a better street built For the designers, a challenge lies in making the work behind the final design visible. Surveys, conversations with communities and coordination across departments all take time, even if the public usually sees only a finished image. "Research is an intangible component, but it eventually drives the project," Shah says. "The government wants to see the 3D renders." Parmar says many government agencies are more familiar with architecture and structural consultancy than with the process urban design requires. "They don't always understand that arriving at an urban-design proposal needs a different kind of process," she says. The team is therefore working on how projects are commissioned and carried out, including surveys, community engagement, procurement and implementation. "We are helping governments redesign the SOPs for how designers should engage with such projects," Parmar says. At Racecourse, their work began by noticing how much road space was devoted to a little-used turn. At Shivananda, they looked at the people squeezing along a narrow footpath beside a large, underused area. In both places, the first step was the same: pay attention to how people live with the city that has already been built, and use that understanding to make it work better for them. All Pictures: Compartment S4

items.descriptionOriginal: Skin-to-skin contact, the practice of a newborn being placed directly onto the mother’s or father’s chest, is considered essential — sometimes lifesaving — care for preterm infants. The World Health Organization recommends it for at least eight hours a day beginning at birth for all babies born before 37 weeks. Incubators can also be critical for these newborns, however, and yet the carefully controlled environments prevent parents from performing that crucial skin-to-skin contact. A pioneering new technology has now bridged the two forms of care, allowing parents to hold their babies to their bodies without disrupting the essential treatments they require. Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital The Skincubator is a wearable medical tool designed for preterm infants weighing under 4.4 pounds that enables prolonged skin-to-skin contact beginning as early as the day of birth. A couple at Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital in Houston, Texas, recently became the first in the U.S. to experience the difference it can make. For about 10 days after their twins were born in August, Tiffany Ikwuagwu and Dorian Ojemen weren’t able to hold the babies, who arrived at just 26 weeks. “This is a great invention,” Ikwuagwu, herself an obstetrician and gynecologist, said in a video from Memorial Hermann upon using the Skincubator. “I think the fact that I can help regulate the babies’ heart[s] and help the babies relax and just have that connection to them, is very special.” Added Ojemen in an interview with CNN earlier this month: “Just the fact that you can have them on your chest, you can look in their eyes, you can hold them, feel them breathe, like, that immediately makes you feel like, wow, I’m a parent.” The tech, which was developed over four years, was granted FDA Breakthrough Device designation last December. With the Skincubator, parents can relax or rest while bonding with their baby for hours at a time, taking turns with other caregivers and family members if they so choose. Infants’ arterial, umbilical, feeding, and airway tubes all remain in place. “The baby is already in their incubator, and they’re transferred from the incubator to the Skincubator while they’re in their isolate,” explained Dr. Jaclyn Ruggiero, principal investigator for an ongoing clinical trial, adding: “The baby’s medical lines and breathing tubes or breathing support are all secured to the Skincubator base. And the way the baby gets into skin-to-skin care is there’s a retractable pad under the baby, and that pad is pulled down slowly.” Children’s Memorial Hermann Hospital Skin-to-skin contact is standard practice for all babies, helping to stabilize their heart rate and breathing, stimulating digestion, regulating temperature, providing protection against infection, and fostering the bond between parent and child. “It turns on a part of the nervous system that’s really important for connection and feeling calm,” Ruggiero said. Per the website, clinicians interested in bringing Skincubators to their NICUs can book a call with the company to begin a pilot program. Learn more. RELATED: Hope Is at the Core of Every Mother Counts’ Mission to Make Childbirth Safe for All

items.descriptionOriginal: “Aha!” moments are great for solving problems but less so for creative judgements, according to new research. We are all familiar with the feeling of “Aha!” that accompanies the sudden realization of our next big ideas. Notably, these insights arrive with a peculiar sense of authority—you don’t just know; you know you know. Decades of research suggest this confidence is usually merited. Across anagrams, riddles, and word problems, solutions that arrive as a sudden Aha! are more likely to be correct than through step-by-step reasoning. Researchers term this finding the Eureka Heuristic, or idea that insights act as cognitive shortcuts, telling us that a given solution is likely to be correct, against our background knowledge. Crucially, past work investigated whether insights predict solution quality in problems with one, verifiable answer. But what happens when there isn’t one? UC Santa Barbara researchers Jacqueline McGuinness, Jonathan Schooler, Shelly Gable ,and Madeleine Gross posed that question in a recent featured article in the Journal of Intelligence . Their answer: in open-ended creative work, the Aha! experience is less a signal of accuracy, and more an illusory sense of brilliance—a phenomenon they refer to as the Aha! glow. “Insights tell us that an idea is promising, but primarily when there is a correct answer to be had,” says McGuinness, manager of Schooler’s META Lab in UCSB’s psychological and brain sciences department. “When we widen the solution space in creative contexts, the feeling of insight can inflate our perception of how good our ideas really are.” Evidence for the Aha! glow first comes from re-analysis of a daily diary study that tracked professional writers and physicists over two weeks. Every night, participants logged their best idea from the day, along with how creative they thought the idea was, and whether or not it came as an “Aha!” moment. Six months later, they were asked to rate the creativity of each idea again. These professions were chosen as real-world proxies for two types of problem-solving. Physicists tend to work on problems with a single, defined solution. Creative writers, in contrast, face problems where many ideas could work, and the value of each only reveals itself once fully developed. The findings revealed a striking difference between professions: writers rated their Aha! ideas as highly creative at the time of idea generation, but much lower 6-months later. On the other hand, physicists rated their Aha! ideas as more creative over time. So when an idea arrives with a flash of insight—an Aha! moment—writers come to think less of it over time, while physicists come to think more of it. Crucially, this divergence only occurred for insights; ideas arrived at through analytical reasoning improved slightly over time for both groups. A second study had 100 participants complete two laboratory tasks: a word problem task with one answer per problem, and the alternate uses task, where participants provide unusual uses for common objects like a brick or tin can. On the alternate uses task, stronger insight experiences predicted how creative people thought their ideas were, much more than creativity judgements of independent raters. Within the same participants, the association between insight intensity and idea quality was nearly four times stronger in the word problem task, compared to the creative idea generation task. “That’s the part I find illuminating,” says Schooler, a distinguished professor of psychological and brain sciences and director of UCSB’s Center for Mindfulness and Human Potential. “For the very same person the experience of aha is well-calibrated to the quality of their ideas on the one task, but produces an Aha! glow on the other.” Yet the team suspects that the glow remains useful. Across both studies, Aha! experiences also predicted greater task enjoyment, confidence, and self-reported motivation to continue working. “In creative work where there is no singular way of assessing solution quality, it often takes months or even years to assess whether an idea will be any good,” adds Gross, a project scientist in the META Lab. “So a boost of confidence, although not always warranted, might be what you need to stick with an idea long enough to find out.” In other words, the researchers say, Aha! moments in creative contexts such as the arts may be less a verdict than a motivational impetus—one that those laboring on ideas unfinished have reason to accept, even if exaggerated. Source: UC Santa Barbara The post ‘Aha!’ moments are good for problem solving, but less helpful for creative work appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Germany just finished building the world’s tallest wind turbine: 1,197 feet tall, and built without a crane. They had to invent an entirely new construction method, because cranes don’t go that high. Also this week: the Hungarian law that fell in the most unexpected way, a Spanish explorer crossing Antarctica on kite power alone, and why fall makes your brain reach for the same reruns every year. Ten solutions total. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement?
