Arielle: So that’s been pretty new. Yeah. I mean, obviously this is a podcast, so people don’t know what I look like regularly, but, uh, I did have hair, and now I don’t, and that’s been very liberating. Mm. But yeah, it is getting colder, so maybe not the most opportune time- I was gonna say … to have an exposed head. But, um, here we are. It’s okay. Uh, just need to get myself, like, a nice little toque, or I guess… Yeah, toque is such a Canadian word, but it’s basically just, like, a beanie. So yeah, I’ll be in the market for some cozy little beanies. But yeah, other than that, nothing really crazy to report. Karissa: Well, that’s a really big change and a very exciting one. Hmm. Um- And it kind of goes with, like, the changing of the seasons as well, so that’s, uh- Yeah. I love it. Arielle: Yeah. The, the, the trees are shedding their leaves, and so am I, in a way. Karissa: Yes. You are also shedding the season away and starting anew. I love it. Arielle: Yeah. And as you said, Karissa, some of our solutions have to do with, uh, changing seasons and nostalgia and all of that. Newsletter & Socials Arielle: But before we get into the solutions, we would love to remind everyone that they can sign up for our free daily or weekly newsletter. You can find the link to sign up for that in the show notes, and that way you’ll get all of this positive news straight to your inbox. Karissa: You can also get all of this positive news on our social media feeds. You can follow us at @optimistdaily on basically everything, except on X, where we are @OdeToOptimism. Arielle: We love it when you guys engage with us, like our stories or posts, share with friends and family, or just on your own personal stories. All of that is really, really appreciated. Your comments, questions, feedback is very welcome. Or you can reach Karissa and I directly at podcast@optimistdaily.com, so feel free to shoot us an email. Karissa: Sharing these solutions in any way possible really helps us out with our mission, and it’s a free way to help The Optimist Daily. But if you’d like to financially support The Optimist Daily, then you can become an Emissary. The link to do that is in the show notes. And Emissaries also get a really cool podcast shout-out to someone or something that makes you optimistic if you sign up. That email with the information on how to do that should automatically go to you, and we send out periodic reminders as well to- Submit your shout-outs. Emissary Shout-out & Local Changemakers Arielle: Yeah, we haven’t really mentioned the Emissary Shout-out recently, because we’ve been focusing on our Local Changemakers series. On that note, we would love to thank everyone who participated and nominated, uh, young local changemakers. This year, we were focusing on changemakers who are 30 years old and under. And it’s been really fun to read all of the submissions. And it has been a little bit difficult to choose our finalists. But we have them, and we are excited to share their stories with you in the coming weeks. Yeah, we’re gonna be starting to publish the Local Changemakers series next week on Wednesday. And we will be featuring a local changemaker every Wednesday into the run-up to Thanksgiving. Karissa: Yeah, I’m so excited to share these stories. And thank you once again to everyone who nominated a young changemaker. Arielle: Mm-hmm. We did get some comments that people were wondering why we were limiting the age. Um, and honestly, in the last two years that we’ve done the Local Changemakers series, I don’t think anyone who was nominated was under the age of 30. Most of the submissions were for people who had established charities or who were just further along, you know, in their lives and professional, uh, experiences. So, that’s why we decided to focus on the younger generation this year. If you wanted to nominate someone who was out of this age range, then there’s always next year for that. Karissa: And we always have our emails open for any suggestions on people to feature on The Optimist Daily. And we sincerely appreciate all of you sharing all the optimism in your own lives with us year-round. Arielle: But speaking of sharing optimism, should I dive into this week’s solutions? Karissa: Yeah, let’s get into all the positive news from this week. Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law Arielle: The first solution is titled “Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law, unlocking billions in EU funds”. Hungary just repealed the law that banned any mention of homosexuality or transgender identities in schools and media, a law Orbán’s government had defended for five years as, quote unquote, “child protection.” The EU had been withholding four point two billion euros over it. And the thing that finally made the law politically toxic for the government wasn’t a rights campaign. It was actually a child abuse scandal. So the political unraveling started when Orbán’s government pardoned someone who had covered up abuse at a children’s home, which turned their own child protection law into a liability rather than an asset. The repeal went further than reversing the 2021 law. It also cleared Hungary’s path to rejoin Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe. Those are major EU research programs that had been suspended along with the funding. The civil rights organization that fought this for five whole years is celebrating, but they’re clear that this isn’t full equality yet. There’s still no same-sex marriage, no adoption rights, and no legal name change process for transgender individuals. But this is a step in the right direction, and we’re here to celebrate every win. How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem Arielle: The second solution is titled “How one small device is solving the apartment solar access problem”. Most people who live in apartments, like me, have been completely locked out of the rooftop solar boom. You can’t just install panels on a building you share with, like, 40 other households. An Australian company built a device that essentially solves that, and it just won the top design award in Australia. We actually talked about Australia’s renewable energy boom last week as well. Karissa: Yeah. Yeah, another, um, win for them is how much renewable energy they were generating on one day, and a lot of that coming from individual solar rooftops. Arielle: SolShare acts as a traffic controller for solar power, automatically reading each apartment’s real-time energy use and routing power from a single rooftop system to whomever needs it. No separate inverters, no complicated wiring per unit, or any of that. Millions of people in Australia live in apartments and have basically no access to rooftop solar benefits until now. There’s been, like, a lot of talk on how to get apartment dwellers involved in solar energy generation. I know that in Spain and I think in Germany, they have these, like, balcony solar panels that you can use. Um, but this one seems even more efficient. Karissa: Yeah. Um, balcony solar is a good approach to this too, but not a comprehensive solution. In California, I know that a bill that allows plug-in balcony solar just got passed, so that’s good because, I mean, there’s a lot of apartments here in this really big state as well. So that will help. But, um, this design could help make everything more efficient. The surprising history of pumpkins Arielle: The next solution is titled “The surprising history of pumpkins: from ancient staple to autumn icon”. So here’s a, a nice, uh, seasonal one for everyone. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: You know pumpkin as the flavor of fall, lattes, and pies, and doorstep decorations, but pumpkin isn’t actually a botanical category. It’s more of a cultural idea that’s been assigned to things for centuries, and for a while in the 1600s, it was a straight-up insult. The whole history- … is weirder and funnier than you’d expect. So the word pumpkin started with the Greeks, and then traveled through French, and landed in English as pompion in the 1500s. It first appeared in print in 1647 as a reference to how poorly early colonists were eating. Not exactly a glamorous origin. By the late 1600s, pumpkin had become an insult. Depending on who was on the receiving end, it meant either conceited and full of hot air or empty-headed. Politicians were getting called pumpkins for hundreds of years, which is funny ’cause I can think of a politician that I could call pumpkin and a lot more. Karissa: I could think of many. Arielle: Um, the reason pumpkins became a fall icon isn’t really about taste. It’s about Americans leaving rural life and then romanticizing what they left. The pumpkin became a placeholder for a simpler agrarian past that was already being lost. So I know I’ve jumped around a lot in describing this article, but you’re just gonna have to read it to, like, really get the flow of the history of the pumpkin. But- Karissa: Hmm … Arielle: you know, pumpkin spice is kind of like a mood for autumn. Um- Yeah … do you have any strong feelings about pumpkins? Karissa: Um, I am just, like, a neutralist when it comes to pumpkin spice, pumpkin-flavored stuff. Like, I think it’s good, but I don’t really, like… I’m not a huge, uh, fan and craving it all year long. When it’s here, it’s here, and I think it’s great, and I’ll grab it sometimes and maybe make something pumpkin flavored. But yeah, I’m just kind of a neutralist. What about you? Arielle: Um, I… Well, now I’m in the Netherlands, and they don’t really have this, like, big pumpkin patch culture in fall. Like, you know when, when people go pick out their pumpkins, and they bring their, like, little babies, and they have… They’re in the field, and da, da, da. I kind of miss that, so I feel like I’m- Hmm … kind of romanticizing the whole pumpkin thing- … uh, just because it’s something that I feel like I’ve lost coming to Europe. But I’m not a huge fan of pumpkin spice, if I’m being honest. I like pumpkin pie. Karissa: Yes, delicious. Arielle: Yeah. Karissa: I love the point you made about, um, you know, the pumpkin patches, being able to go to small family farms. Because those local farms, they get a real economic boost from this time of year with the pumpkin season tourism. So whether it’s just taking the family to go get your seasonal photos or going to take advantage of the cool stuff that pumpkin patches have to offer, whether it’s corn mazes or pumpkin carving. I mean, I live in an agricultural area, so I’m familiar with the pumpkin patch culture. It makes me pretty nostalgic ’cause I definitely grew up doing that. And like you said, Arielle, you have to check out the article for more. A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss Arielle: The next article is titled “A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss”. A startup in the Netherlands has developed a concrete coating that grows its own moss. No soil or irrigation. There’s no structural modifications. You just apply it to an existing wall, and the moss colonizes it on its own. They’ve already put it on warehouses, noise barriers, social housing, and bridge piers in Amsterdam, and one of those applications is specifically to deter graffiti. And I actually think I’ve passed one of these, like, in my neighborhood, um, and I just didn’t realize that that’s what it was until I read this article. Yeah. So how it works is that the moss attaches through tiny thread-like structures that grip the surface without penetrating it. So you can apply this to existing facades without any structural work. It’s a coating, not a construction project. In Amsterdam, they’re testing it out on bridge piers specifically as a graffiti deterrent, which is not a use case I saw coming. Research shows wet moss cools through evaporation the same way trees do in cities, but dry moss in direct sunlight overheats, so placement and climate really matter for how well it works. Urban greening is a major climate adaptation strategy right now, and the main barriers have always been cost and maintenance, so this solution addresses both at once. Karissa: I love that, you know, it doesn’t require, like, new construction. It can just be applied to already existing structures in cities where it gets a lot of moisture, like Amsterdam. I’m sure that this can be a really great addition. World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand the reins over to Karissa is “World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany”. Germany just completed the world’s tallest wind turbine, 365 meters tall, taller than Berlin’s TV tower, which is also very tall. They couldn’t use a crane to build it because cranes don’t go that high, so they invented a new way to do it. But honestly, the most significant part isn’t the height, it’s the proposal to add thousands of these above existing wind farms without using a single square foot of new land. As I mentioned, traditional cranes couldn’t reach, so they built like a telescoping inner tower that raises itself through a surrounding lattice structure. The construction method is as novel as the turbine itself. Germany has around 30,000 existing wind turbines, and the proposal is to place taller ones above or alongside them rather than finding new land, which sidesteps one of the biggest political fights in wind energy, which is people don’t wanna give up the land. GICON, the engineering firm that built this turbine, says, uh, this design could generate roughly twice the electricity of conventional turbines with comparable rotors because winds at 300 meters are faster and more consistent. But commissioning isn’t until November, so the real world numbers aren’t in just yet. As I said, land use is one of the biggest political obstacles to wind expansion. There’s, like, a lot of not in my backyard fights that have stalled projects for years. But stacking vertically rather than spreading horizontally reframes the whole conversation Karissa: All right. Well, I’ll take it from here, Arielle. Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns Karissa: Heading back into the whole fall idea, the next article is “Fall nostalgia: why your nervous system reaches for reruns when autumn arrives”. The urge to rewatch your comfort show every October isn’t just a personality quirk. There’s a real psychological reason your nervous system steers you toward reruns when fall arrives. Something about the season registers as a small form of loss, and your brain responds by reaching for the familiar. I mean, I’ve definitely had this feeling before. And before I go any further, Arielle, is there anything that you rewatch every fall or find yourself, uh, reaching for? Arielle: When Harry Met Sally. Karissa: Yes. That one is very, very fall indeed. Arielle: Yeah, I don’t know. I just, I love the aesthetic. And yeah, I guess I never really noticed that I always wanna watch that particular movie once, like, the leaves start to change and stuff. Karissa: Yeah. For me, I always go back to Taylor Swift’s Red album in the fall. And it’s very, like, a fall-coded album in general, but it came out in the fall when I was, like, in junior high, and it always brings me back to that time of year. And it sometimes makes me feel a little bit, like, sad too because I start missing that time in my life. In general, your body recognizes fall through a whole bunch of sensory clues. There’s wood smoke, October light, the sound of a school bus, and that’s what takes me back to Red. Arielle: Mm-hmm. Karissa: But the same memory system that holds pre-verbal experiences from early childhood is also at play here when you experience all these, these autumn, um, these autumn- Arielle: Sensations Karissa: things. Yeah, sensations is exactly the word. Psychologists say we prefer reruns in the fall because our brains favor predictability when things feel uncertain. And you already know how it ends, so that matters a lot more than you’d think. Nostalgia isn’t just about these warm, fuzzy feelings. It can also hold a lot of grief, and looking backward is a part of how we integrate the past and then move forward. So there is a psychological reason why we want to indulge in this fall nostalgia. Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Karissa: Okay, the next solution is, “Is this nut the most underrated sleepy-time snack? Here’s what the sleep research says”. Apparently pistachios contain their own melatonin. They don’t just offer compounds that help your body make melatonin, they produce it themselves. A nutritional review found that one small handful covers five different sleep-related nutrients at once, which is a pretty unusual thing to find in any single food. Pistachios have more vitamin B6 than any other tree nut, and B6 is the co-factor your body needs to convert tryptophan into serotonin, into melatonin. So there’s a whole chain reaction happening from that one handful, and there’s a little bit more of the science behind it in the article. The thing is that there hasn’t been a clinical trial that has actually tested pistachios directly for sleep yet, and the review was partially funded by American Pistachio Growers, so there might be a little bit of a bias here. But in an era where sleep is kind of one of the biggest wellness obsessions right now, and there’s magnesium supplements, mouth tape, weighted blankets, people are really desperate for anything that helps with sleep. Arielle: Yeah, I really like the food as medicine angle. It’s getting way more mainstream, so people aren’t just thinking about sleep hygiene habits. They’re also starting to ask what they should be eating. And I think food is definitely underrated, especially, um, in North America as- Karissa: Mm-hmm … Arielle: as an impactful solution to some of your health issues. Um- Yeah … so even though there’s no clinical trial yet, I think it’s, it’s worth more seriously considering food as a way to help you out with whatever health or wellness issues you’re struggling with. How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration Karissa: The next solution is kind of a fun one, “How kites and ancient design are replacing fuel in Antarctic exploration”. A Spanish explorer just left for Antarctica on a sled powered entirely by kites. No engine, no fuel. The last time someone made a comparable crossing, they burned through 45,000 gallons of diesel. But this sled is built on ancient Inuit design principles that this, uh, researcher has been refining for 25 years, and NASA is also along for the ride. So again, this vehicle draws from Inuit sled design and goes back to ancient indigenous knowledge. This technology is something that’s been used for thousands of years. There’s a number of onboard research projects on this kite-powered sled. One of them is a NASA study asking whether salt rocks on Antarctica’s surface could harbor microbial life. The four crew members themselves on this kite-powered sled are also research subjects. A psychologist is monitoring their isolation, sleep, and social dynamics for 85 days to generate data for future space missions. There are such harsh conditions out there, so being able to refine and use this kite technology is pretty interesting. And of course, it’s important to use sustainable science in exploration. New research identifies the exact spot where Alzheimer’s protein tangles lock in Karissa: The next solution is “New research identifies the exact spot where Alzheimer’s protein tangles lock in”. We- researchers at Northwestern and UC Santa Barbara, go Gauchos, that’s where I went, have identified the specific point on a tau protein where the misfolding that causes Alzheimer’s begins. It’s not somewhere vague in the brain, it’s the exact molecular anchor point, down to which amino acid, so really pinpointing here. And blocking that one spot in lab experiments actually stops the spread of Alzheimer’s, so this could be a very important piece of the puzzle. The mechanism that the researchers found is called dock-and-lock. The misfolded tau docks at one specific spot first, then the rest of the protein snaps into the wrong shape, and blocking just that one anchor point inhibited fiber growth in experiments. This research is part of a broader shift towards molecular level targeting in neurodegenerative disease, identifying the exact mechanism rather than trying to clear a protein broadly. There’s still a gap between, you know, pinpointing this spot and being able to create a drug that actually does something about it. But of course, the research has to come first, so we’re happy to recognize this progress. The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model Karissa: Moving on to our final solution of the week, we have “The Giving Grove: how Kansas City’s free community orchards became a national model”. 13 years ago, someone planted a small orchard on the corner of a shuttered school in Kansas City, and today that idea has grown into 14,000 trees across 847 orchards in 17 cities, which means that more than a million people live within walking distance of a free fruit tree. Kansas City now has more community orchards than any other city in the country. It has nearly 250 of them. The reason 80% of these orchards are still productive, which is genuinely high for grassroots urban agriculture, is that the organization didn’t just plant trees and leave them, they built a stewardship network of 1,700 trained orchard caretakers across the country. This kind of reminds me of a solution I- we just shared about, um- Some trees planted in Germany, and they have, like, a whole app in, you know- Arielle: Mm, yeah Um- So that citizens could also take care of the trees and give them water when they, when they needed it. Karissa: Mm-hmm. Yeah, I love this, uh, citizen agriculture movement. So cool. These orchard caretakers operate on about a million dollars a year and only go where they’re invited. Communities have to request orchards, so the model has held up because they don’t impose the model at all. The idea is spreading across to other cities. San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York are now in discussions to join this trend of community orchards. So it’s actively scaling, and it’s a, you know, a very hyper-local solution that individual communities can focus on and implement themselves. Arielle: And it really addresses the issue of food access. Um- Karissa: Mm-hmm. Arielle: Food access equity is a real issue right now. There’s food deserts. There’s rising produce costs. There’s diet-related chronic illnesses, and this kind of a solution that you mentioned, it’s low-tech, it’s hyper-local, um, and it’s pretty permanent. I think this can address a lot of those issues. I know that urban agriculture has been having a cultural moment, but a lot of urban agriculture is focused on, like, boutique rooftop gardens, and- Karissa: Yeah Arielle: you know, not everyone has access to that. So a community orchard serving everyday neighborhoods is a different category, and I can just imagine, like, rocking up to a tree and picking a fruit off of it- … and eating it. That… It’s also so satisfying. Karissa: Okay. Well, that’s all the positive news we had from The Optimist Daily this week. Positive Quote & Wrap-up Karissa: Before we log off for the day, we have a positive quote to share with you. Arielle: This one’s from E.B. White, the author of Charlotte’s Web, one of my childhood favorites. Okay, so the quote says, “Hang on to your hat, hang on to your hope, and wind the clock, for tomorrow is another day.” We will be back next week with more solutions, but until then, we hope you enjoy your weekend. Karissa: Yeah. Bye, everyone! Arielle: Bye! The post Podcast Transcript October 23rd, 2026— Hungary repeals anti-LGBTQ law, world’s tallest wind turbine, and why fall makes you reach for reruns first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.titleOriginal: Could tiny robots replace open-heart surgery?
items.description: Οι επιστήμονες δημιούργησαν ρομπότ στο μέγεθος μιας μύτης μολυβιού που προορίζονται να ταξιδέψουν μέσα στο σώμα για να μεταφέρουν φάρμακα σε λοιμώξεις μέσα σε μια καρδιά που χτυπά. Τα ρομπότ, που σχεδιάστηκαν για να αντικαταστήσουν την επικίνδυνη χειρουργική επέμβαση ανοιχτής καρδιάς και την αναποτελεσματική ενδοφλέβια θεραπεία με φάρμακα για τη θεραπεία απειλητικών για τη ζωή καρδιακών λοιμώξεων, θα μπορούσαν επίσης να χρησιμοποιηθούν για τη λιγότερο επεμβατική και ακριβέστερη θεραπεία άλλων…
items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have created robots the size of a pencil tip intended to travel through the body to deliver medicine to infections inside a beating heart. The bots, designed to replace risky open-heart surgery and ineffective IV-drug therapy to treat life-threatening heart infections, could also be used to less invasively and more precisely treat other hard-to-reach diseases, including cancer. “With just a little pinprick, you insert a micro robot and do a procedure without infection or blood loss. And you don’t need to have a surgeon operating it to get the drugs robustly, safely, and efficiently to the right place,” says senior author Axel Krieger, a medical roboticist known for creating robots that perform surgery without human help. “There’s a lot of areas beyond heart infections where this kind of targeted drug therapy and these kinds of steerable robots could play a major role. It’s really the frontier of surgical robotics.” The work appears in Advanced Materials Technologies . Each year about 50,000 people in the United States contract endocarditis, a heart tissue infection. The typical treatment is a weeks-long course of intravenous antibiotics, which often fails because the drugs are too diluted by the time they reach the heart. Doctors are then left with two risky choices—prescribing more and higher doses of antibiotics, which can be toxic, or extremely risky open-heart surgery. To get the drugs directly to the infected heart tissue, the team developed magnetically-powered robots called “millirobots,” because of their size—they’re as wide as a pencil tip or a matchstick head, and about as long as a grain of rice. The robots work in pairs. There’s one the team calls the needle module, which gently latches onto heart tissue right at the infected site. There it serves as a docking station, waiting right on the beating heart for the drug module. The drug module carries medicine to the docking station, where it magnetically docks and slowly releases the antibiotics right where they’re most needed. Both robots are magnetic and guided wirelessly by an external electromagnetic coil system that works like an MRI machine. Having two tiny robots instead of one larger one allows the device to reach tight spots in the body. The needle can remain docked while the drug module is replaced, allowing for repeat doses of medicine if needed. “Magnetic guidance is exciting because you don’t have to power the robot itself. It doesn’t carry batteries and motors,” Krieger says. “The drugs can be delivered safely, with technology like the gradients and fields in an MRI. But instead of using it for imaging, it drives the millirobots.” The researchers successfully tested the robots on phantom heart models that closely mimic a human heart, and on real porcine heart tissue. The robots traveled smoothly and autonomously, even against simulated blood flow. “We can just inject a robot with a little pill into your vein where it travels to the site, right to where we really need to deliver the drugs, and it’s minimally invasive,” says first author Anuruddha Bhattacharjee, a former Johns Hopkins postdoctoral student who is now an assistant professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham. In addition to eliminating the need for open-heart surgery, drug treatment with the robots could take hours instead of weeks. “Usually if you do IV drug treatment, you need four to six weeks of therapy. But with these robots the entire procedure might take 10 minutes—maybe an hour if you want to do a couple rounds,” Bhattacharjee says. “If everything works well, you go from four to six weeks of treatment to one day or less.” The team also believes the robots would be helpful delivering targeted medications to fight cancer where it’s spreading. The researchers next plan to test the robots in more realistic phantom hearts, with muscle contraction and the beating movement of a real heart. The work was supported by the National Science Foundation’s Foundational Research in Robotics CAREER program. Additional authors are from Johns Hopkins, the University of Maryland, and Weinberg Medical Physics. Source: Johns Hopkins University The post Could tiny robots replace open-heart surgery? appeared first on Futurity .

items.title: Στα 82 της, Αυτή η γιαγιά οδηγεί ποδήλατα και οδηγεί τρακτέρ
items.titleOriginal: At 82, This Grandma Rides Bikes and Drives Tractors
items.description: Στα 74 της αποφάσισε να μάθει κάτι νέο. Σήμερα στα 82 της κάνει ποδήλατο, τρακτέρ και μοιράζεται τις περιπέτειές της στα social media! Το ταξίδι της Σούχμα ξεκίνησε όταν ένα αστείο μετατράπηκε σε μια μυστική περιπέτεια μάθησης ανάμεσα σε αυτήν και ένα μέλος της οικογένειας. Μακριά από την υπόλοιπη οικογένεια, έκαναν εξάσκηση μαζί μέχρι που τελικά έμαθε να ιππεύει. Οκτώ χρόνια αργά…
items.descriptionOriginal: At 74, she decided to learn something new. Today, at 82, she rides a bike, drives a tractor and shares her adventures on social media! Sukhma’s journey began when a joke turned into a secret learning adventure between her and a family member. Away from the rest of the family, they practised together until she finally learnt to ride. Eight years later, she’s doing much more than riding a bike. She drives a tractor and runs her own social media page, sharing reels of herself riding. She didn’t learn because she had to. She learnt because she wanted to. Sukhma’s story reminds us that curiosity has no expiry date, and age doesn’t have to stop us from trying something we’ve always wanted to do. items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "How Does It Work?" — The Better India's series that takes the everyday things you see, use and rely on, and uncovers the clever technology, design and sustainable thinking that makes them work better. From the objects in your home to the systems around you, we break down the ideas behind them in simple, easy-to-understand language. Because innovation isn't always about futuristic machines or complicated technology. Sometimes, it's hiding in the things we use every day. Look at a satellite image of a cyclone, and you will see enormous bands of clouds spiralling over the ocean. What looks like a swirling mass of white clouds is actually a complex weather system, powered by warm seawater and shaped by winds moving thousands of metres above the Earth. Predicting where this storm will travel, how strong it will become, and whether it will make landfall is no small feat. Yet, today, satellites and artificial intelligence (AI) are helping scientists make these forecasts faster and more accurately, giving communities valuable time to prepare. In India, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) uses satellites such as INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR to monitor cyclones. In 2025, satellite imagery helped track weather systems, including Cyclone Montha, which crossed the Andhra Pradesh coast as a severe cyclonic storm. But how do machines in space and AI models on Earth work together to forecast a storm that has not yet reached the coast? Step 1: Satellites keep an eye on the ocean The first step is observation. Geostationary weather satellites orbit approximately 36,000 km above the equator, moving at the same rate as the Earth's rotation. This allows them to continuously observe the same broad region, capturing changes in cloud formations and atmospheric conditions. India's INSAT-3D and INSAT-3DR satellites monitor clouds, atmospheric moisture and temperatures to track developing storms. Photograph: ( The Week ) India's INSAT satellites use specialised sensors to capture visible-light and infrared images, as well as information about water vapour in the atmosphere. Unlike ordinary cameras, infrared sensors can measure temperatures even at night, helping scientists identify the cold, high cloud tops associated with powerful thunderstorms. Scientists look for clues such as clusters of thunderstorms, curved cloud bands and the beginnings of a rotating system. Other satellite instruments measure ocean temperatures, rainfall and wind-related conditions, helping meteorologists understand whether the environment is becoming favourable for a cyclone. Think of it as watching a storm's earliest movements from above, even when it is far out at sea and beyond the view of coastal observers. Step 2: AI learns to recognise weather patterns Collecting data is only half the job. Scientists must also work out what it means for the storm's future. This is where AI comes in. AI weather models are trained using decades of historical weather observations , atmospheric measurements and records of past storms. By studying these examples, they learn relationships between variables such as wind speed, air pressure, humidity and temperature. For instance, a model may learn that certain combinations of atmospheric conditions and ocean temperatures have previously been associated with a storm strengthening or changing direction. AI models analyse historical weather data to learn patterns in wind, pressure and temperature. Photograph: ( CNET ) It is a little like learning to recognise a familiar pattern in a jigsaw puzzle. The AI compares the current conditions with patterns it has learnt, then estimates how the weather could evolve. Google DeepMind's WeatherNext Cyclones is one example. Its model combines global weather information with historical cyclone records to forecast a storm's path, intensity and wind structure. In 2025, its forecasts helped the US National Hurricane Center anticipate Hurricane Melissa's rapid intensification and landfall in Jamaica. Step 3: The AI runs multiple possible futures Here is where the technology becomes particularly useful. Weather is a constantly changing system. A small difference in wind direction or atmospheric pressure can alter a cyclone's eventual path . So, instead of treating one prediction as certain, advanced AI models can generate multiple possible scenarios. This technique is called ensemble forecasting . Imagine a cyclone moving towards the eastern coast of India. One forecast might show it turning north, another might suggest it moving towards the northwest, while others may predict different speeds or intensities. Ensemble forecasting generates multiple possible storm tracks, helping meteorologists assess uncertainty. Photograph: ( FOX Weather ) By comparing these possible tracks, meteorologists can identify areas that are more likely to be affected and understand where uncertainty remains. WeatherNext Cyclones can generate 1,000 possible scenarios in less than a minute on specialised computing hardware. Its forecasts can extend up to 15 days ahead, although uncertainty generally increases the further into the future a prediction looks. Step 4: Forecasters turn predictions into warnings AI does not replace meteorologists. Instead, its predictions complement satellite observations, conventional weather models and expert analysis. Forecasters assess the available evidence before issuing official warnings about a cyclone's likely track, strength, rainfall and landfall. These warnings help authorities plan evacuations, fishermen return to shore, and emergency teams prepare shelters and supplies. The goal is not to predict every movement perfectly. It is to reduce uncertainty early enough for people to act. Early warnings help coastal communities prepare, fishermen return to shore and authorities organise evacuations. Photograph: ( facebook/@TheMech Mind) As satellites collect more detailed observations and AI models become better at interpreting them, cyclone forecasting continues to improve. Every additional hour of reliable warning can give vulnerable communities more time to protect homes, secure essential supplies and move to safety. A cyclone may be impossible to control, but understanding its likely path is becoming easier. And that growing ability to see a storm coming is one of the most important ways technology can help save lives. Sources: 'Cyclone Track Forecasting Based on Satellite Images Using Artificial Neural Networks' by Rita Kovord nyi and Chandan Roy. 'How Satellites Track Hurricanes' by National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service 'How we're supporting better tropical cyclone prediction with AI' by Google Deep Mind.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Provincial Tree Pageant Reminds Communities to Honour Their Big Trees Reading Time: 2 minutes Ontario’s Tree Trust celebrates a rare, century-old Cucumber Tree in St. George, honoring one family’s decades of stewardship and the community’s growing love for mature trees. In recent years, the Ontario government has significantly reduced environmental protection legislation. Increased development with minimal consequences threatens the province’s biodiversity, habitat, and once-protected natural character. But people are fighting back. Despite the current lack of legislation, environmental communities continue to raise awareness and push their cause. Tree Trust , a not-for-profit, grassroots organization that focuses on mature tree protection, is one of them. Education, advocacy, and community engagement are Tree Trust’s core values. Based in Elora, Tree Trust launched in 2019 and now extends to 12 communities, with chapters run entirely by volunteers. In addition to offering educational events like tree walks and talks, Tree Trust works with ISA-board-certified arborists committed to improving the health and longevity of mature trees. Protecting mature trees is essential to urban communities. Many are older than most community members, and these legacy trees offer immediate, irreplaceable benefits to our cities. Increased health and mental well-being, stormwater reduction, climate change mitigation, and economic benefits are all reasons to invest in big trees. One way Tree Trust does this is by welcoming the province to participate in the Ontario Tree Pageant. This engaging, inviting competition reminds the province that a love of trees goes far beyond the surface. For the past three years, hundreds of nominations have been received, special stories have been shared, and majestic trees have been recognized. This year’s esteemed panel of judges chose a tree that represents togetherness, a tree that is beloved and highlights a story of community awareness and environmental stewardship. This year’s winner is a Cucumber Tree ( Magnolia acuminata ), estimated to be over 100 years old, standing tall in St. George. This year’s winning tree was nominated by St. George resident and artist, Meredyth Kutt. This endangered, Ontario-native specimen stands among many other trees and is over 75 centimeters in diameter. Photo courtesy of Tree Trust . This tree is being recognized not only for being a unique and endangered species, but also for its history. Researchers at the University of Guelph have studied this individual for its ability to thrive outside its expected range. Some even say it is the farthest west mature Cucumber Tree in Canada. Beyond its uniqueness, this tree is celebrated as the epitome of environmental and community connection. The Kutt family, the tree’s owners, have stewarded it for over 20 years. They have cultivated a second Cucumber tree and currently support six of the original’s progeny. This cucumber tree’s story is exactly the kind of stewardship Tree Trust wants to support. The Ontario Tree Pageant gives people a platform to share special stories about trees that mean the most to them. It reminds us how connected we are to nature and that, for all these big trees give us, they deserve to be celebrated. The post Provincial Tree Pageant Reminds Communities to Honour Their Big Trees appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.description: Το Diwali είναι μια εποχή για να φωτίσουμε τα σπίτια μας με ντιγιά, αλλά το να γιορτάσουμε το φεστιβάλ βιώσιμα μπορεί να ξεκινήσει με κάτι τόσο χωρίς προβλήματα όπως η επαναχρησιμοποίηση αυτού που ήδη έχουμε. Η δημιουργός του lifestyle και των ταξιδιών Sharon JM Nathani, η οποία μοιράζεται ιδέες για DIY στο Instag…
items.descriptionOriginal: Diwali is a time to light up our homes with diyas , but celebrating the festival sustainably can begin with something as hassle-free as reusing what we already have. Instead of buying new earthen lamps every year, a little creativity can help give old diyas a fresh look. Lifestyle and travel creator Sharon JM Nathani, who shares DIY ideas on Instagram through her page @thatangloindiansindhi, suggests a simple way to reuse diyas from the previous year and make them ready for the festive season. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sharon JM Nathani || Lifestyle & Travel Creator (@thatangloindiansindhi) A trick to keep the wicks in place Her method involves using desi ghee and candles to prepare the diyas for lighting. She recommends heating the ghee, melting the candles into it, and pouring the mixture into the diyas before placing the wicks. This small change in the process makes a difference. Often, when the wicks are placed inside the diya before the liquid is poured, they can fall over or become crooked while filling. Sharon suggests pouring the mixture first and adding the wick afterwards, helping it stay upright and in place. Once the diyas are ready, you can add a little glitter or finely cut flower petals to decorate them. These small touches can give old lamps a festive makeover without the need to purchase new ones. Reusing diyas is an easy way to reduce waste during the festive season while making the most of items already at home. With a little effort, last year's lamps can return to your Diwali decorations, bringing the same festive warmth without adding to unnecessary consumption. This Diwali, before heading out to buy new decorations, take a look at what you already have. Sometimes, the most sustainable festive ideas begin with giving familiar things another chance.

items.description: Ξαφνικά ο Darth Vader ανεβαίνει σε μια καρέκλα μπροστά από το Hôtel de Ville στο Παρίσι. Ντυμένος στα μαύρα, κουνάει το σπαθί του σαν μαέστρος, ενώ 200 μουσικοί και εθελοντές, οι περισσότεροι γύρω στα είκοσι, ετοιμάζονται. Ξεπακετάρουν τα όργανά τους: βιολιά, τσέλο, κλαρίνα. Τότε ο πραγματικός μαέστρος, Étienne Jarrier, ανεβαίνει σε ένα πράσινο sh…
items.descriptionOriginal: S uddenly Darth Vader climbs up onto a chair in front of the Hôtel de Ville in Paris. Clad in all black, he swings his sword like a conductor’s baton while 200 musicians and volunteers, most in their early twenties, get ready. They unpack their instruments: violins, cellos, clarinets. Then the real conductor, Étienne Jarrier, steps up in a green shirt and the musicians of the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde (New World Orchestra) begin to play. Their song is a poignant one — El Pueblo Unido Jamás Será Vencido (The People United Will Never Be Defeated), a Chilean protest song written in the 1970s by the composer and pianist Sergio Ortega and folk group Quilapayún. It has since become an international hymn of resistance, and the members of the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde chant its refrain again and again to support the student protests in France this October, voicing their solidarity with the half million young people who are protesting high living costs and deteriorating conditions in their schools. “Music is a way for us to be heard,” says 25-year-old Jarrier, who co-founded the orchestra in 2022 “to find new ways forward.” A self-described “member of the climate generation,” the young man with the red-tinted black locks says he felt that climate activism had exhausted most avenues of protests and found it was time for “artivism,” art as a vehicle for political expression, “as a way of reaching people at the deepest level.” The post How ‘Artivism’ Is Driving the Resistance in Paris appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News PANORAMA Builds Replicable Conservation Solutions Database Spanning Nearly 1,900 Case Studies Worldwide Reading Time: 3 minutes A decade-old platform now hosts 1,897 conservation solutions from over 1,300 contributors, turning local environmental successes into replicable conservation solutions database entries anyone can adapt. For over ten years, PANORAMA – Solutions for a Healthy Planet has pursued a deceptively simple mission: build a global community where changemakers share, adopt, and scale up what already works. Rather than compiling passive success stories, this replicable conservation solutions database structures each entry as adaptable building blocks, distilling complex projects into stepwise blueprints practitioners elsewhere can actually apply to their own contexts. The scale is substantial. PANORAMA now hosts 1,897 documented solutions from 1,327 contributing organizations and individuals across 11 thematic communities spanning restoration, species conservation, marine and coastal ecosystems, One Health, protected areas under the 30×30 framework, and nature-culture heritage sites. This solutions database aligns explicitly with major global directives, including the Kunming-Montréal Global Biodiversity Framework, the Paris Agreement, and the UN’s 2030 Agenda, translating local action into evidence that supports international sustainability commitments. What distinguishes each entry within this replicable conservation solutions database is methodology rather than mere documentation. Every solution unpacks the how and why behind an effective environmental initiative, breaking successful projects into essential components others can adapt rather than simply admire. Solutions must be practical and tailored to specific scenarios, relevant to sustainability frameworks, proven through real-world results, and flexible enough for varied environments and sectors. Recent additions illustrate this approach in practice. In Mongolia, pastoral communities facing recurrent droughts and dzud , severe winter disasters causing catastrophic livestock losses, needed climate-resilient infrastructure. The UN Development Programme (UNDP) ADAPT Project responded by establishing 48 hay and feed storage facilities across four climate-vulnerable provinces, using risk assessments combining climate, vegetation, and livestock mortality data to identify optimal locations. The solution strengthened emergency fodder reserves while improving herders’ adaptive capacity against increasingly unpredictable seasons. Around Lake Victoria, shared by five East African nations and supporting over 45 million people through fisheries, water supply, and agriculture, declining water quality made coordinated basin management nearly impossible without shared evidence. The Lake Victoria Basin Commission, supported by GIZ, developed the first-ever State of the Basin Report, combining water quality sampling at 44 stations across three countries with consultations spanning all five partner states. This replicable conservation solutions database entry identifies wetland rehabilitation, reforestation, and catchment restoration as the most cost-effective pathways toward improved water quality, now serving as a shared baseline for planning across the entire basin. PANORAMA’s replicable conservation solutions database documents how five East African nations built a shared State of the Basin Report for Lake Victoria and how a multi-stakeholder partnership restored Ethiopia’s Lake Hawassa, both now scaled into national and regional policy frameworks. Photo by David Munyasa on Pexels. In Ethiopia’s Rift Valley, Lake Hawassa faced accelerating degradation from deforestation, pollution, erosion, and rapid urbanization, pressures no single actor could address alone. A multi-stakeholder partnership uniting public authorities, private companies, and civil society applied a Natural Resources Risk and Action Framework developed between 2015 and 2020, jointly assessing risks and implementing nature-based solutions. The partnership succeeded so thoroughly that it transitioned to full government management and scaled into federal guidelines, now restoring water bodies nationwide. This replicable conservation solutions database operates through a partnership network spanning 12 organizations, including GIZ, IUCN, UNDP, GRID-Arendal, UNEP, Rare, EcoHealth Alliance, ICCROM, the World Bank Group, OCTO Group, ICOMOS, and IFOAM. Together with over 1,000 individual solution providers representing institutions worldwide, this network forms the backbone connecting grassroots knowledge to global policy forums, ensuring diverse local perspectives genuinely influence international environmental decision-making rather than remaining isolated success stories. Peer-to-peer exchange sits at the platform’s core philosophy. Rather than treating conservation knowledge as proprietary or locked within academic journals, this replicable conservation solutions database transforms tacit, hard-won field experience into explicit, shareable wisdom. A coordinator from the Fiji Locally Managed Marine Area Network described the platform as compelling solution providers to examine their own work more critically, improving quality and scalability specifically because their solutions will be judged against a global standard for replicability. The database’s cross-cutting scope extends far beyond conservation biology alone. Communities addressing gender mainstreaming, financing mechanisms, governance structures, technology for nature conservation, and geodiversity all coexist within the same searchable platform, filterable by ecosystem type from agro-ecosystems to urban built environments, and by region spanning Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania, and the Coral Triangle. As climate and biodiversity crises intensify simultaneously, the pressure to avoid reinventing solutions grows correspondingly urgent. This replicable conservation solutions database offers exactly that efficiency: proven building blocks from Mongolian herders, East African basin commissions, and Ethiopian multi-stakeholder partnerships, structured so practitioners facing similar challenges elsewhere can adapt rather than start from zero, accelerating the pace at which local innovation becomes global practice. The post PANORAMA Builds Replicable Conservation Solutions Database Spanning Nearly 1,900 Case Studies Worldwide appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: A Legal Secretary Rode the Subway to Work for 67 Years. Nobody Knew She had $9M.
items.description: Για 67 χρόνια, η Sylvia Bloom οδηγούσε το μετρό για τη δουλειά, ζούσε σε ένα διαμέρισμα που ελέγχεται από το ενοίκιο και περπάτησε μέσα από χιονοθύελλες στα 96 αντί να φτιάχνει ταξί -- όλα αυτά ενώ έχτιζε αθόρυβα μια περιουσία 9 εκατομμυρίων δολαρίων αντικατοπτρίζοντας τις μετοχές των αφεντικών της με μισθό γραμματέα. «Ήταν γραμματέας σε μια εποχή που έτρεχαν τη ζωή του αφεντικού τους, συμπεριλαμβανομένης της προσωπικής τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: For 67 years, Sylvia Bloom rode the subway to work, lived in a rent-controlled apartment, and walked through blizzards at 96 rather than hail a cab -- all while quietly building a $9 million fortune by mirroring her bosses' stock trades on a secretary's salary. "She was a secretary in an era when they ran their boss' lives, including their personal investments," her niece explained, and Bloom simply applied that same attentiveness to her own future, one modest purchase at a time. She never mentioned it to anyone - not colleagues, possibly not even her husband -- because, as her niece recalled, "she didn't think it was anybody's business but her own." What she did think was her business was what happened to it after she was gone: nearly all of it went to scholarships for students who couldn't afford college, becoming the largest individual gift in Henry Street Settlement's 125-year history. There is something clarifying about a life like hers -- the discipline kept private, the wealth worn invisibly, the generosity revealed only at the end, as if the whole thing had been a very long, very patient act of faith in someone else's future.

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Ερευνητές στο Πανεπιστήμιο Northwestern και στο UC Santa Barbara εντόπισαν ένα συγκεκριμένο σημείο επαφής στις πρωτεΐνες tau όπου ξεκινά η λανθασμένη αναδίπλωση που οδηγεί τη νόσο του Αλτσχάιμερ. Το εύρημα, που δημοσιεύτηκε στο Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, υποδηλώνει ότι ο ιστότοπος θα μπορούσε να στοχευτεί με φάρμακα που έχουν σχεδιαστεί για να…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Researchers at Northwestern University and UC Santa Barbara identified a specific contact point on tau proteins where the misfolding that drives Alzheimer’s disease begins. The finding , published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , suggests the site could be targeted with drugs designed to slow tau tangle growth in the brain. How tau proteins misfold In healthy brains, tau proteins stabilize the internal scaffolding of nerve cells. In tauopathies , including Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia, tau misfolds and recruits healthy proteins to adopt the same abnormal shape. The result is fibrillar aggregates: knotted threads that accumulate and spread through brain tissue. What happens the moment a newly produced tau protein first encounters an existing tangle wasn’t well understood. To find out, chemist Songi Han and colleagues at Northwestern used nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to track engineered tau as it attached to pre-existing tau fibers, watching individual regions as the process unfolded. The region around amino acid 300 stood out because it made contact with existing aggregates faster than any other site examined, acting as an initial anchor. The rest of the protein then aligned to the fiber’s structure. The team calls it “dock-and-lock”: tau docks at the contact point first, then the remaining sections fall into place. Where water comes in The anchor’s stickiness wasn’t fully explained by the protein’s structure. Molecular simulations and water dynamics experiments added a piece: the region around amino acid 300 has an unusual arrangement of water molecules that are easy to dislodge when another tau molecule gets close. That displacement lowers the energy cost of attachment and nudges the docking forward. Chemically blocking the anchor site inhibited fiber growth. Blocking other positions had much less effect. That gap in response is what gives the finding traction as a potential drug target. A possible drug target “Once you know that aggregation-prone tau proteins always have a hotspot that is first attracted to the same site of tau that is stacked to fibrils, then you know there’s always some part of the protein that you can target to neutralize,” said Han. “If you know where to block its action of misfolding, you could block it to prevent it from propagating.” The experiments used a shortened tau construct with a disease-associated mutation, not full-length tau from human tissue , so translation to disease conditions isn’t established. The anchor point’s location may also shift between tau variants and disease types. Whether the mechanism holds across different tau structures, and whether it can be safely disrupted in a living brain, are the next questions. Source study: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences- A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation Did this solution stand out? items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Είναι ώρα συγκομιδής στο Κάνσας Σίτι και στην Ακαδημία του Κάνσας Σίτι, οι μαθητές βγαίνουν έξω κατά τη διάρκεια του γεύματος για να μαζέψουν τζίτζιφι κατευθείαν από τα δέντρα. «Νιώθω σαν μια πριγκίπισσα του παραμυθιού κάθε μεσημεριανό γεύμα», είπε η Νόβα Χένρι, ηλικιωμένος, «επειδή βγαίνω έξω και απλά γεύομαι μικρές λιχουδιές». Τα δέντρα είναι δωρεάν για οποιονδήποτε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It is harvest time in Kansas City, and at Kansas City Academy, students are stepping outside during lunch to pick jujubes straight off the trees. “I feel like a fairy tale princess every lunch,” said Nova Henry, a senior, “because I get to go out and just feast on little treats.” The trees are free for anyone to take from. That is the whole premise of the Giving Grove , a Kansas City organization 14 years into planting fruit orchards on vacant land and asking nothing in return. It now has 14,000 trees in 847 orchards across 17 cities, and more than a million people live within walking distance of one. The Giving Grove’s origin story The Giving Grove began with a small stand of trees planted 13 years ago on the corner of a shuttered public school in the Waldo neighborhood. The school has since reopened and is expanding, so the original orchard is currently behind a construction fence, but it is still there. “This little orchard we’re standing in here started a national movement,” said Giving Grove Marketing Director Sarah Sikich. “I think it’s one of Kansas City’s best-kept secrets.” From that corner, the organization partnered with Kansas City Community Gardens to spread orchards across unused plots throughout the metro, from a few trees on a school parking lot to plots with over a hundred. Kansas City now has 248 free orchards with nearly 4,600 fruit, nut, and berry trees. “I joke that Kansas City should be the city of orchards, not the city of fountains,” Sikich said. “No other city in the United States has as many orchards as we do.” Built on shared knowledge More than four out of five Giving Grove orchards remain in production. The reason, according to founder Kevin Birzer, is that the organization never just plants trees and walks away. “It’s stuff people can learn, but it takes a long time, and it’s not really efficient for one group to do that,” he said. “So our thought from day one was we would provide that expertise, the knowledge of how to grow the trees , how to select the trees.” About 1,700 “orchard stewards” across the country maintain that relationship. The Giving Grove offers training, workshops, help finding grants, soil improvements, pruning support, and succession planning for when stewards move on or burn out. Janet Porter, a science teacher who tends the orchard at Kansas City Academy, has found the same to be true. “They do training. They do workshops. If I ever have any questions, they’re just a phone call away.” It is not just fruit, either. The trees attract insects , which attract songbirds, which attract predators like hawks. At least one Kansas City student turned pruning experience into a job at a tree nursery. A model spreading city by city Nine years ago, a community gardening group in St. Louis asked for help, and the Giving Grove said yes. Now the organization is in cities across the country, with conversations underway about San Francisco, Minneapolis, and New York City. Different communities want different trees, and growing in Brooklyn is not the same as growing in Utah, especially without chemical pesticides or herbicides. “Some environments are more challenging,” Birzer said. “Creating something really cool for the neighborhood, that part’s universal.” The Giving Grove runs on just over $1 million a year. Most of it comes from 1% for the Planet , a network that channels one percent of member businesses’ annual revenue toward environmental causes; corporations sometimes add volunteer labor, and individual donors fill in the rest. The organization only enters communities that invite it, and right now it is working through a backlog of those invitations. “I think people have an easy time falling in love with what we’re doing,” Sikich said. “Planting fruit trees is something everyone can agree with.” Did this solution stand out? items.description: Είναι κολίβριο, γεράκι ή σκόρος; Το κάπως συγκεχυμένο όνομα κολιμπρί είναι (drumroll, παρακαλώ) ένα είδος σκώρου που μεταναστεύει στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο και την Ιρλανδία από τη Νότια Ευρώπη και τη Βόρεια Αφρική κάθε καλοκαίρι. items.descriptionOriginal: Is it a hummingbird, a hawk, or a moth? The somewhat confusingly named hummingbird hawk-moth is (drumroll, please) a moth species that migrates to the U.K. and Ireland from southern Europe and North Africa each summer. Its moniker comes from the way it feeds — hovering over flowers like a hummingbird. Wildlife photographer Andrew Fusek-Peters captured that feeding process earlier this month in a series of stunning photos that show the 2-inch insect beating its wings at a staggering 85 times a second while drinking from a valerian bush in his garden in Shropshire, England. Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS The striking moths have been thriving in the U.K. thanks to the warm summer. James Benwell, from the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, told the BBC that 2026 was a “record year” for sightings in the country. “They’ve had a really good year this year,” he said. “Normally they would come in small numbers. We’d normally hear of a few maybe. But this year, we’ve seen loads of records of them.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS Though it borrows its name from the hummingbird, this hawk-moth actually has the avian species beat when it comes to hovering speed — hummingbirds average about 50 beats per second, while the insects can hit up to 85 beats per second. (Another fun fact: Hummingbirds are native only to the Americas, and hummingbird hawk-moths only to the U.K., Europe, and North Africa.) “The hummingbird hawk-moth is a summer visitor to the U.K. from southern Europe and North Africa but can be seen in most months of the year and is a favorite garden visitor,” Fusek-Peters told SWNS. “With warmer summers, it now breeds in the U.K. and will often overwinter here and can now be considered a U.K. breeding species.” He noted that the bugs “emit an audible hum” as they hover. “It means that it can maneuver easily with its long proboscis able to delve into deeper flower stems such as red valerian.” Andrew Fusek-Peters / SWNS As for how he captured such action-packed photos, Fusek-Peters said it took time and experimentation. “I spent much of the summer photographing them and experimented with slowing down my shutter speed to capture the incredible motion and orange flash of the wings.” This article was originally written by Ed Chatterton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Reading Time: 2 minutes How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment Driving more safely doesn’t just benefit road users. Many of the habits associated with safer driving can also reduce a vehicle’s environmental impact by lowering fuel or energy consumption and cutting harmful emissions . While wider developments in vehicle technology and transport policy play an important role, individual driving habits remain part of the picture. How smoother driving can cut fuel use and emissions According to Energy Saving Trust, efficient driving techniques such as smooth acceleration, staying within speed limits and avoiding unnecessary braking can help reduce fuel consumption and emissions. This means anticipating traffic conditions and maintaining a steady speed wherever it’s safe and practical to do so. Frequent acceleration and harsh braking require more energy than gradual speed changes. In petrol and diesel vehicles, this typically means burning more fuel. In electric vehicles, it can increase battery consumption and reduce driving range. Why speed, braking and forward planning matter Safe driving is closely linked to awareness and anticipation. Giving yourself more time to react to changing road conditions can help reduce sudden manoeuvres that increase fuel consumption and vehicle wear. For example, noticing traffic slowing ahead allows you to ease off the accelerator gradually instead of braking heavily at the last moment. Likewise, anticipating junctions and changing speed limits is key. Drivers looking to improve their awareness may find that utilising telematics insurance to help you be more aware of your driving style encourages more consistent habits, as many telematics systems monitor factors such as braking, acceleration and cornering behaviour. Look after the vehicle as well as your driving style Environmentally responsible driving is not solely about behaviour behind the wheel. Keeping your vehicle in good mechanical condition can also support efficiency and help emissions-control systems operate as intended. Regular servicing allows potential issues to be identified before they affect vehicle performance. Maintaining correct tyre pressures can reduce rolling resistance, while replacing worn components when required can help the vehicle run more efficiently. Drivers should also address dashboard warning lights promptly and ensure emissions-related components are functioning correctly. A poorly maintained vehicle may consume more fuel or energy than necessary. Motoring experts regularly highlight the importance of maintenance as part of environmentally conscious driving, alongside habits such as reducing unnecessary vehicle weight and keeping tyres correctly inflated. Put greener driving into the UK’s bigger environmental picture The UK’s transition towards lower-emission transport involves multiple factors, including advances in vehicle technology and public policy. However, driver behaviour still plays a role. If millions of motorists adopt more efficient driving habits, the combined effect can contribute to lower fuel consumption and reduced emissions across the vehicle fleet. While no individual action can solve environmental challenges on its own, small changes across a large population can support wider sustainability goals. The post How Safer Driving Techniques Can Benefit the Environment appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Reading Time: 3 minutes How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams Retail teams work across different stores, shifts, and job roles, so training must stay accessible during busy working days. Sales associates need product knowledge, supervisors need management guidance, and every employee must complete required safety courses. A dependable training platform helps meet these demands without disrupting daily store operations. A Learning Management System (LMS) brings these needs into one trackable program. The right retail LMS software also gives leaders a clearer view of participation, assessment results, and unresolved gaps, creating a practical foundation for consistent store training. The following areas outline what to consider when choosing a system. Create One Training Hub For Every Store A retail LMS gives employees one place to access onboarding, product updates, customer service lessons, and compliance courses. A retail LMS software directory helps decision-makers compare systems built for retail requirements, including mobile access, short lessons, progress tracking, and reporting. Centralized content reduces inconsistent instructions between locations and lets training leaders update a course without distributing new files manually. Store teams also benefit from clear learning paths. A new sales associate can complete orientation, point-of-sale training, and product lessons in sequence. A department supervisor can follow a separate path covering coaching, scheduling, inventory procedures, and incident reporting. Deliver Training Around Store Schedules Retail employees rarely share the same hours, making classroom sessions difficult to coordinate. Mobile access lets employees complete assigned lessons between shifts, during scheduled training time, or at another approved location. Short lessons support this schedule. A five-minute module can explain a product feature, customer greeting standard, or safety procedure without removing an employee from the sales floor for a long session. Managers can assign content by role, location, or employment stage, so each learner receives relevant material. A Learning Management System also records completion automatically. Managers do not need separate spreadsheets for each store, which reduces manual follow-up and gives regional leaders a consistent record. Keep Product And Service Knowledge Current Retail information changes often. Product lines, prices, promotions, return rules, and service expectations require regular updates. A central course library lets training teams revise a lesson once and publish the current version across selected stores. Knowledge checks give managers more than a completion mark. Short quizzes can test whether employees understand product differences, warranty conditions, or escalation procedures. Assessment results show where a team needs a refresher before a new promotion begins. Store leaders can also use assigned learning for seasonal hiring. Temporary employees receive the same essential service and safety information as permanent staff, with a clear deadline before their first scheduled shift. Track Compliance Without Manual Chasing Retail organizations must monitor courses related to workplace safety, data protection, harassment prevention, and other internal requirements. An LMS records assignments, due dates, completions, and assessment results in one system. Automated reminders help employees address overdue courses before managers need to contact each person. Escalation reports show which store, role, or department needs attention. These records also give training leaders evidence that required instruction was assigned and completed. Access controls support accurate reporting. A district manager can review assigned stores, while a store manager sees the employees within that location. This structure keeps reports useful without giving every user access to unnecessary information. Use Reports To Improve Store Performance Completion data helps leaders measure participation, but useful reporting goes further. Scores, attempts, time spent, and course status reveal whether employees understood the material or rushed through it. Training leaders can compare results by location or role to find recurring gaps. If several stores perform poorly on a product assessment, the lesson needs clearer explanations or better examples. If one location has low completion rates, managers can review scheduling, communication, or access problems. Learning data also supports regular management routines. Regional leaders can review a monthly report, discuss overdue assignments with store managers, and adjust upcoming training according to business needs. Give Managers A Practical Coaching Tool An LMS supports daily coaching when managers connect online lessons with store activity. After an employee completes a customer service module, a supervisor can observe a customer interaction and discuss the result privately. Managers can assign refresher lessons after an observed gap. They can also recognize completed development paths during one-on-one meetings and use assessment results to plan the next coaching conversation. This approach keeps training connected to job behavior. Employees receive instruction, practice the skill, and discuss progress with a manager instead of treating courses as isolated administrative tasks. Conclusion Retail LMS software gives store teams a shared training structure without forcing every employee into the same schedule. The strongest implementation starts with role-based learning paths, mobile-friendly lessons, current product content, and compliance tracking. Training leaders should audit existing courses, group them by role and store need, then select a system that reports completion and assessment results clearly. A small pilot across several locations provides useful evidence before wider deployment. The post How Retail LMS Software Can Support Training Across Store Teams appeared first on Happy Eco News .
